title: The First Stone Tools: the Oldowan
summary: Early humans in East Africa strike sharp-edged flakes from stones, beginning the Stone Age.
text: The oldest stones that can be identified with certainty as tools come from Gona in Ethiopia and are about 2.6 million years old; the technique is named after the Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania. Using a hammerstone, early humans such as Homo habilis struck sharp flakes from cobbles and used them to strip meat from bones and to crack bones open for the nutritious marrow. Even older finds from Lomekwi in Kenya, roughly 3.3 million years old, suggest that pre-human species were already working with stones. Toolmaking is regarded as the beginning of the Stone Age and as a decisive step in human development.

title: Homo erectus Leaves Africa
summary: The first human species to do so, Homo erectus spreads from Africa through the Near East as far as East Asia.
text: About 1.8 million years ago, groups of Homo erectus reached the Caucasus, as the skull finds from Dmanisi in Georgia show. Over hundreds of thousands of years the species spread as far as Java and China, where it became known as Java Man and Peking Man, and later into Europe as well. An upright, enduring walker with a large brain, it made hand axes and learned to use fire. Homo erectus survived for roughly 1.8 million years, making it the longest-lived human species.

title: Mastery of Fire
summary: Early humans learn to use fire deliberately and to keep it burning.
text: By about 400,000 years ago at the latest, humans of the species Homo erectus and their descendants were using fire regularly, as hearths in Africa, Israel and Europe show. Fire provided warmth and light, protected against predators and made food more digestible and more energy-rich through cooking. The shared fire became the center of the group and probably encouraged language and social life.

title: The Emergence of Homo sapiens in Africa
summary: Anatomically modern humans evolve in Africa.
text: The oldest known fossils of Homo sapiens come from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco and are about 300,000 years old. Genetic studies confirm that all people alive today trace back to African ancestors. Modern humans were distinguished by a large brain, a flat face and a lightly built skeleton, and they produced increasingly refined tools.

title: Art and Ornament from Blombos Cave
summary: In South Africa, the oldest known geometric engravings and shell beads are created.
text: In Blombos Cave on the southern coast of South Africa, archaeologists found pieces of ochre engraved with diamond patterns, pierced snail shells worn as bead necklaces, and finely worked bone tools and spear points. The finds are around 75,000 years old, and a cross-hatched drawing made with ochre is about 73,000 years old. There was also a toolkit for mixing paint in abalone shells from a layer 100,000 years old. The cave shows that Homo sapiens was already thinking symbolically in Africa, long before cave art appeared in Europe.

title: Out of Africa
summary: Groups of Homo sapiens leave Africa and spread across Asia and Europe.
text: About 70,000 to 60,000 years ago, small groups of modern humans migrated through the Near East into Asia and reached Europe around 45,000 years ago. There they encountered Neanderthals, with whom they occasionally interbred, as traces in the genomes of people today show. Within a few tens of thousands of years, Homo sapiens had settled almost the entire Old World.

title: The Settlement of Australia
summary: Humans reach the Australian continent by boat or raft.
text: At least 50,000 years ago, and according to some finds as early as 65,000 years ago, people crossed open stretches of sea from Southeast Asia to Australia. This is the earliest evidence of deliberate seafaring. Over tens of thousands of years the ancestors of the Aboriginal peoples developed a distinctive culture whose rock art is among the oldest artwork of humankind.

title: The Cave Paintings of Lascaux
summary: Ice Age hunters paint hundreds of animals on the walls of a cave in southern France.
text: Discovered by teenagers in 1940, the cave of Lascaux in the Dordogne contains around 600 paintings and more than 1,000 engravings of horses, aurochs, deer and bison. The artists used pigments of ochre, charcoal and manganese ore and worked by the light of fat lamps. The images probably had religious or ritual meaning and show that people of the Old Stone Age were capable of symbolic thought and art.

title: The Invention of Pottery
summary: Hunter-gatherers in East Asia fire the first clay vessels, long before farming begins.
text: The world's oldest potsherds come from Xianrendong Cave in southern China and are about 18,000 to 20,000 years old; only slightly younger are finds from Japan, where the Jōmon culture later produced elaborately decorated vessels. Their makers were not yet farmers but hunters, fishers and gatherers who cooked food and stored supplies in clay pots. In the Near East and Europe, pottery only took hold with settled life around 7000 BC. Ceramics are especially important for archaeology because they last almost indefinitely and their shapes and patterns make individual cultures recognizable.

title: The Settlement of the Americas
summary: People from Siberia reach North America across the Bering land bridge.
text: During the last Ice Age, sea levels were so low that a land bridge existed between Siberia and Alaska. Across it and along the Pacific coast, people migrated into the Americas and reached the southern tip of the continent within a few thousand years. The Americas were thus the last great landmass to be settled; the Indigenous peoples of the Americas descend from these migrants.

title: Göbekli Tepe: the Oldest Monumental Structures
summary: Hunter-gatherers in southeastern Anatolia erect stone circles with pillars weighing several tons.
text: On the hill of Göbekli Tepe near the modern city of Şanlıurfa in Turkey, people built circular enclosures around 9500 BC from T-shaped stone pillars up to five meters high, carved with reliefs of animals. The builders still lived mainly by hunting and gathering. The site shows that communal sanctuaries may have arisen before farming and may have helped set the move toward settled life in motion.

title: The Neolithic Revolution in the Fertile Crescent
summary: People begin to grow grain and keep animals, and become settled.
text: In the Fertile Crescent between the Levant, Anatolia and the Zagros Mountains, people began after the end of the Ice Age to cultivate emmer, einkorn, barley and lentils and to breed sheep, goats, cattle and pigs. Instead of moving from place to place, they now lived permanently in villages of mud-brick houses. The shift to a farming way of life is regarded as one of the most profound changes in human history.

title: Jericho: One of the Oldest Settlements with a Wall
summary: A large permanent settlement grows up at a spring in the Jordan Valley and receives a stone wall and a tower around 8000 BC.
text: Jericho, today's Tell es-Sultan in the West Bank, was permanently settled around 9000 BC and soon grew to several hundred, perhaps more than a thousand inhabitants. Around 8000 BC the inhabitants surrounded their settlement with a stone wall and built a tower almost nine meters high with an internal staircase, the oldest known structure of its kind. Whether the wall served as protection against enemies or against floodwater and mud is disputed. Also famous are the plaster-covered skulls that represented ancestors and were kept in the houses. Jericho is considered one of the oldest continuously inhabited settlements in the world.

title: The Large Settlement of Çatalhöyük
summary: One of the largest settlements of the Neolithic, with several thousand inhabitants, arises in Anatolia.
text: Çatalhöyük in central Anatolia was inhabited between about 7100 and 5700 BC and at times housed up to 8,000 people. The mud-brick houses stood packed together without streets and were entered through the roof by ladder. Wall paintings, bull skulls and female figurines offer insight into religious beliefs; the inhabitants practiced farming, kept livestock and traded in obsidian.

title: The First Irrigation Farming in Mesopotamia
summary: Farmers channel river water onto their fields and make the dry land between the two rivers fertile.
text: In the regions along the middle Tigris there was too little rain for farming, but around 6000 BC villages of the Samarra culture such as Tell es-Sawwan and Choga Mami began to lead river water onto their fields through ditches. Artificial irrigation allowed two harvests a year, the cultivation of flax and grain, and larger settlements. Canals had to be dug, cleaned and shared collectively, which required agreement and leadership. On this foundation the world's first cities arose in southern Mesopotamia in the 4th millennium BC.

title: The Beginning of Metalworking: the Copper Age
summary: People learn to smelt copper ore and cast metal; the first copper axes, pins and ornaments appear.
text: Native copper was already being cold-hammered in Anatolia around 8000 BC, but only around 5000 BC did smelting ore in furnaces succeed: the oldest evidence comes from Belovode in Serbia, shortly afterwards from Iran and Anatolia. The mines of Rudna Glava and the gold finds from the cemetery of Varna in Bulgaria show how quickly metal became a mark of wealth. Copper was soft and only of limited use for tools, but the knowledge of smelting and casting paved the way for the Bronze Age. In Europe this transitional period is called the Copper Age, and it was the age in which Ötzi lived.

title: The Domestication of the Horse
summary: On the steppes of Central Asia, people begin to keep, milk and ride horses.
text: In settlements of the Botai culture in present-day Kazakhstan, researchers found large numbers of horse bones dating to around 3500 BC, traces of mare's milk in clay vessels, and wear on teeth suggesting the use of bits. Genetic studies show, however, that today's domestic horses descend from a different population from the steppes north of the Black Sea, which spread rapidly around 2200 BC. The horse fundamentally changed mobility, warfare and trade: riders and chariots shaped the Bronze Age, and pastoral peoples of the steppe were able to control vast territories.

title: The Invention of the Wheel
summary: The first wheels and wagons appear almost simultaneously in Mesopotamia and Europe.
text: Around 3500 BC the oldest evidence for wheels appears: as a potter's wheel in Mesopotamia and as a wagon wheel in images and finds from the Near East to Central Europe. Solid wooden disc wheels on axles made ox-drawn carts possible and eased the transport of harvests, building material and goods. Together with the plow and copper working, the wheel began the transition to the advanced civilizations of the Bronze Age.

title: Ötzi Dies in the Alps
summary: A man of the Copper Age dies at the Tisenjoch pass and is preserved in the ice for more than 5,000 years.
text: In 1991, hikers at the Tisenjoch pass in the Ötztal Alps found the glacier mummy of a man who had died around 3300 BC. An arrow in his shoulder shows that he was killed. His clothing of fur and grass, his copper axe, bow and arrows, and the contents of his stomach provide unique information about life, diet and technology at the end of the Neolithic.

title: The Emergence of Sumerian Cuneiform
summary: In the city of Uruk, the Sumerians develop the oldest known writing system.
text: Around 3200 BC, scribes in Uruk began to record payments and stores with pictorial signs on clay tablets. The pictures became abstract signs pressed into damp clay in wedge shapes with a reed stylus. Cuneiform was used for more than 3,000 years for Sumerian, Akkadian, Hittite and other languages, and it transmitted laws, contracts, myths and the Epic of Gilgamesh.

title: The Unification of Egypt
summary: Upper and Lower Egypt are united under a single pharaoh.
text: According to tradition, King Menes, who is probably identical with the ruler depicted on the Narmer Palette, united the Nile Valley from the First Cataract to the Delta. He is said to have founded the capital Memphis. This marked the beginning of pharaonic Egypt, which lasted with brief interruptions for almost three millennia and is divided into more than 30 dynasties.

title: Megalithic Monuments and Stonehenge
summary: Neolithic farmers in Western Europe build burial chambers, stone rows and stone circles from blocks weighing many tons.
text: From about 4500 BC onward, people along the Atlantic coast from Portugal to Scandinavia built tombs and ritual sites from large stones, known as megaliths, among them the stone rows of Carnac in Brittany, the passage tomb of Newgrange in Ireland and the temples of Malta. Stonehenge in southern England began around 3000 BC as a circular ditch with wooden posts; around 2500 BC the sarsen stones, weighing up to 25 tons, were raised, while smaller bluestones came from Wales, 250 kilometers away. The monument is aligned with the sunrise at the summer solstice and probably served as a sanctuary and burial place. Structures like these required the cooperation of many communities over generations.

title: The City-States of Sumer and the Standard of Ur
summary: In Sumer, city-states such as Ur, Uruk and Lagash compete for land and water; the royal tombs of Ur attest to their wealth.
text: In the 3rd millennium BC, Sumer was divided into a dozen city-states whose kings fought one another over canals, border land and supremacy; the Stele of the Vultures from Lagash depicts one of these wars. In the 1920s the British archaeologist Leonard Woolley uncovered the royal tombs of Ur, in which rulers had been buried with gold helmets, lyres, jewelry of lapis lazuli and dozens of sacrificed attendants. The so-called Standard of Ur, a box inlaid with shell and lapis lazuli, shows war with chariots on one side and a banquet with tribute on the other. The finds offer insight into kingship, craftsmanship and long-distance trade in the early city-states.

title: The Building of the Great Pyramid of Khufu
summary: The largest structure of antiquity is built at Giza as the tomb of the pharaoh Khufu.
text: The Great Pyramid of Giza was originally about 146 meters high and consists of roughly 2.3 million blocks of stone. It was built in some 20 years by thousands of workers who were not slaves but paid and provisioned laborers. As the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing, it testifies to the skill of Egyptian builders in planning, mathematics and organization.

title: The Flowering of the Indus Civilization
summary: Planned cities such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa arise along the Indus.
text: The Indus Civilization extended across present-day Pakistan and northwestern India and covered a larger area than Egypt and Mesopotamia. Its cities had streets laid out at right angles, fired bricks, wells, baths and a sophisticated drainage system. The Indus script has still not been deciphered; around 1900 BC the cities declined, probably because of climate change and shifting rivers.

title: Sargon of Akkad Founds the First Empire
summary: Sargon subdues the Sumerian city-states and creates the first empire of Mesopotamia.
text: Sargon, who according to legend was abandoned as a foundling in a reed basket, conquered the city-states of Sumer around 2334 BC and extended his rule as far as Syria and Anatolia. He made Akkadian the language of administration and installed governors of his own. The Akkadian Empire lasted about 150 years and became the model for all later empires of Mesopotamia.

title: The Epic of Gilgamesh
summary: The tales of King Gilgamesh of Uruk are written down and become the oldest great epic in world literature.
text: Sumerian poems about Gilgamesh were written down around 2100 BC during the Third Dynasty of Ur; around 1200 BC the scribe Sin-leqi-unninni combined them in Babylonian into an epic on twelve tablets. It tells of the king's friendship with the wild Enkidu, of the fight against the monster Humbaba and of Gilgamesh's futile search for immortality after his friend's death. The eleventh tablet contains a flood story resembling the biblical account of Noah. The epic was copied in scribal schools from Anatolia to Palestine and was rediscovered in London in 1872 among tablets from the library of Ashurbanipal.

title: The Middle Kingdom of Egypt
summary: After a period of collapse, Mentuhotep II reunites Egypt; a flowering of literature, administration and land reclamation follows.
text: After the collapse of the Old Kingdom and some 150 years of division, the Theban king Mentuhotep II reunified the country around 2055 BC. The kings of the 12th Dynasty, such as Senusret III and Amenemhat III, secured Nubia with fortresses, had large areas of the Fayum drained, and strengthened the officialdom against the nobility. The Middle Kingdom is regarded as the classical age of Egyptian literature, with works such as the Story of Sinuhe and the instructions for kings and officials. Around 1650 BC the Hyksos, who came from western Asia, took power in the Nile Delta and brought the horse and the chariot to Egypt.

title: Minoan Civilization on Crete
summary: With palaces such as Knossos, the first advanced civilization in Europe arises on Crete.
text: From about 2000 BC the inhabitants of Crete built large palace complexes at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia, with hundreds of rooms, storage magazines, water pipes and brightly colored wall paintings of dolphins, bull-leapers and women in elaborate robes. The Minoans, named after the legendary King Minos, carried on sea trade as far as Egypt and Syria and wrote in Linear A, a script still undeciphered today. The absence of fortifications and of depictions of war is striking. The enormous volcanic eruption on the island of Thera around 1600 BC and the Mycenaean takeover around 1450 BC ended their heyday; Arthur Evans excavated Knossos from 1900 on.

title: The Code of Hammurabi
summary: King Hammurabi of Babylon has an extensive collection of laws carved in stone.
text: On a stele of black diorite more than two meters high, Hammurabi had some 280 legal rulings recorded, covering family, property, trade, wages and punishments. The penalties depended on social rank and followed in part the principle of an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth. The stele was found at Susa in 1901 and stands today in the Louvre; it is one of the oldest and most complete collections of law in the world.

title: Rise of the Hittite Empire
summary: From their capital Hattusa the Hittites rule Anatolia and northern Syria and become a great power alongside Egypt.
text: Around 1650 BC King Hattusili I made the mountain stronghold of Hattusa in central Anatolia his capital; his successor Mursili I even sacked Babylon in 1595 BC. The Hittites spoke the oldest Indo-European language preserved in writing, adopted cuneiform and left behind at Hattusa an archive of more than 30,000 clay tablets containing laws, treaties, rituals and myths. Their chariots and their early ironworking made them feared warriors; under Suppiluliuma I and Muwatalli II they struggled with Egypt over Syria. Around 1200 BC the empire collapsed in the turmoil of the Bronze Age collapse, and Hattusa was abandoned.

title: Mycenae and Mycenaean Civilization
summary: On the Greek mainland warrior princes build citadels such as Mycenae and Pylos and administer them using the Linear B script.
text: From about 1600 BC fortified palace citadels arose in Greece at Mycenae, Tiryns, Pylos and Thebes, whose rulers were buried in shaft graves with gold masks and weapons. The Mycenaeans took over much from the Minoans but were more warlike: walls of blocks weighing many tons, the Lion Gate of Mycenae and beehive tombs testify to their power. Their script Linear B, deciphered in 1952 by Michael Ventris, proved to be an early form of Greek and served to record stores, craftsmen and levies. Heinrich Schliemann excavated Mycenae in 1876 and believed he had found the world of Homer; around 1200 BC the palaces were destroyed, and Greece sank into a dark age.

title: The Shang Dynasty and the Oracle Bones
summary: In China the first archaeologically attested dynasty begins, with bronze casting and the oldest Chinese characters.
text: The Shang dynasty ruled the valley of the Yellow River from about 1600 to 1046 BC. Its kings consulted the ancestors by heating ox shoulder blades and turtle shells and interpreting the cracks; the questions incised on them are the oldest evidence of Chinese writing. Elaborate bronze vessels, chariots and the royal tombs at Anyang reveal a highly developed and strictly ordered society.

title: The Lapita Culture Settles the Pacific Islands
summary: Seafarers with outrigger canoes set out from Southeast Asia and reach the remote islands of Melanesia and Polynesia.
text: Around 1500 BC groups from the region of Taiwan and the Philippines pushed out through the Bismarck Archipelago into the open Pacific. They are recognizable by their stamped pottery, named after the site of Lapita in New Caledonia, and carried pigs, chickens and dogs as well as taro and yams in their canoes. Within a few centuries they reached Fiji, Tonga and Samoa, from where their descendants, the Polynesians, much later settled Hawaii, Easter Island and New Zealand. Navigating by stars, swells and the flight of birds across thousands of kilometers ranks among the greatest achievements in the history of seafaring.

title: Akhenaten's Religious Reform
summary: Pharaoh Akhenaten raises the sun disk Aten to be the only god and founds a new capital.
text: Amenhotep IV took the name Akhenaten, banned the worship of the old gods, above all Amun, and had a new residence, Akhetaten, built near present-day Amarna. The art of this period shows the king and his wife Nefertiti in an unusually natural and intimate manner. After his death Egypt returned to the old cults under Tutankhamun and erased Akhenaten's name from the monuments.

title: The Battle of Kadesh and the First Peace Treaty
summary: Egyptians and Hittites fight over Syria with thousands of chariots and later conclude the oldest surviving peace treaty.
text: At Kadesh on the Orontes the armies of Ramesses II and of the Hittite king Muwatalli II clashed in one of the largest chariot battles in history. Ramesses only narrowly escaped defeat but had the battle portrayed in his temples as a brilliant victory. Some 15 years later Ramesses and Hattusili III concluded a treaty of peace and mutual assistance that survives on silver tablets and clay tablets and is regarded as the first peace treaty in world history.

title: The End of the Bronze Age and the Sea Peoples
summary: Within a few decades the Hittite Empire, the Mycenaean palaces and many trading cities collapse.
text: Around 1200 BC the Hittite Empire, the palaces of the Mycenaeans in Greece and cities such as Ugarit were destroyed or abandoned; Egypt fended off attacks by the so-called Sea Peoples only with difficulty. The causes are thought to be a combination of droughts, famines, earthquakes, uprisings and the breakdown of the trade networks for tin and copper. The crisis was followed by a dark age, out of which a new world emerged with iron tools and the alphabet of the Phoenicians.

title: The First Ironworking and the Beginning of the Iron Age
summary: After the collapse of the Bronze Age, iron, which is more readily available, becomes the standard material for weapons and tools.
text: Individual iron objects made of meteoric iron are known as early as the 3rd millennium BC, and the Hittites produced small quantities of forged iron in the 14th century BC. Only when the trade routes for tin broke down around 1200 BC did smiths in Anatolia, Cyprus and the Levant turn on a larger scale to smelting iron ore in bloomery furnaces and improving the metal into steel by carburizing and hardening. Iron ore was available almost everywhere, so plowshares, axes and swords became cheaper. From the Near East the technique spread to Greece, Europe and India and, independently of this, to Africa south of the Sahara.

title: The Olmecs in Mesoamerica
summary: The first advanced civilization of the Americas arises on the Gulf coast of Mexico.
text: From about 1200 BC the Olmecs built centers such as San Lorenzo and La Venta, with earthen pyramids, plazas and colossal heads of basalt weighing many tons. They grew maize, carried on long-distance trade in jade and obsidian, and played a ritual ball game. The calendar, the pantheon and the architectural forms of the Olmecs went on to influence the later cultures of the Maya and the Aztecs, which is why they are regarded as the mother culture of Mesoamerica.

title: The Phoenicians and Their Alphabet
summary: The trading cities of Tyre, Sidon and Byblos develop an alphabet of 22 letters and carry it across the whole Mediterranean.
text: Around 1050 BC the Phoenicians on the coast of present-day Lebanon simplified older consonant scripts of the Levant into an alphabet of only 22 signs that anyone could learn in a short time; the inscription on the sarcophagus of King Ahiram of Byblos is one of the earliest examples. As skilled seafarers and traders in purple dye, cedar wood, glass and metals, they founded settlements on Cyprus and Sicily, in Spain, and in 814 BC Carthage in North Africa. The Greeks adopted their letters and added vowels, the Etruscans and Romans passed them on; the Aramaic, Hebrew and Arabic scripts also derive from the Phoenician alphabet.

title: The Kingdom of Kush in Nubia
summary: South of Egypt an independent African kingdom with its capital at Napata arises on the Nile.
text: Nubia, in what is now Sudan, was rich in gold and lay on the trade routes for ivory, ebony and incense. After the earlier kingdom of Kerma, which had been conquered by Egypt around 1500 BC, the Kingdom of Kush formed from about 1000 BC at Napata by the fourth cataract of the Nile. Its kings worshipped the god Amun at the sacred mountain Jebel Barkal and adopted hieroglyphs and pyramid tombs, yet remained culturally distinct. Around 730 BC the Kushite king Piye conquered Egypt and founded the 25th Dynasty of the Black Pharaohs; later Kush moved its capital to Meroe and lasted into the 4th century AD.

title: Rise of the Neo-Assyrian Empire
summary: From Ashur and Nineveh the Assyrians conquer the entire Near East with the most powerful army of their day.
text: From 911 BC the kings of Assyria on the upper Tigris extended their rule through annual campaigns; Ashurnasirpal II built Nimrud into a magnificent residence, and Tiglath-Pileser III created a standing army and a system of provinces. The Assyrians deployed siege engines, cavalry and iron weapons, deported subjugated peoples and deliberately spread terror through reliefs and inscriptions. At its height in the 7th century BC the empire reached from Egypt to Iran; at Nineveh, Ashurbanipal assembled the first great library, with more than 30,000 clay tablets, among them the Epic of Gilgamesh. In 612 BC Babylonians and Medes destroyed Nineveh, and the empire collapsed.

title: The Chavín Culture in Peru
summary: In the Andes, Chavín de Huántar becomes a pilgrimage center whose art and religion shape large parts of Peru.
text: Chavín de Huántar lies at an altitude of more than 3,000 meters in the Peruvian Andes, at the confluence of two rivers. From about 900 BC the people there built a temple of stone with underground passages, water channels and the Lanzón, a stone pillar four and a half meters high bearing the image of a deity with the fangs of a predator. Pilgrims from across the Andean region brought shells from the coast, obsidian and textiles; in the temple, priests played shell trumpets and used hallucinogenic cacti in rituals. The Chavín style, with jaguars, snakes and eagles, spread through pottery, gold and textiles and is regarded as the first shared culture of the Andes, out of which the Moche, Nazca and Inca later emerged.

title: The First Olympic Games
summary: The first recorded contests in honor of Zeus are held at Olympia.
text: According to tradition the first games were held in 776 BC at Olympia in the Peloponnese; the only event was a race the length of the stadium. Every four years athletes came together from across the Greek world, and a sacred truce was in force for the duration of the games. The Greeks reckoned time in Olympiads, and the games were not banned until AD 393, by the Christian emperor Theodosius.

title: The Founding of Rome
summary: According to legend, Romulus founds the city of Rome on the Tiber.
text: According to Roman tradition, Romulus, who is said to have been suckled by a she-wolf, founded the city of Rome in the year 753 BC. Archaeologically, settlement of the hills by the Tiber can be traced from the 10th century BC. The Romans counted their years from this date of foundation, ab urbe condita.

title: Greek Colonization of the Mediterranean
summary: Greek cities found hundreds of colonies from Spain to the Black Sea and spread the language, writing and way of life of the Greeks.
text: Shortage of land, hunger, trade and internal conflict led many poleis to send out citizens and found new cities: Cyme and Syracuse in Italy and Sicily, Massalia, today's Marseille, Cyrene in North Africa, Byzantion on the Bosporus and numerous cities on the Black Sea. The colonies were politically independent but remained tied to their mother city through cults, language and trade. Southern Italy and Sicily thus became Magna Graecia, Greater Greece, where thinkers such as Pythagoras and Archimedes were active. Colonization brought the Greeks into contact with Etruscans, Celts, Scythians and Egyptians and passed the alphabet and the coin on to their neighbors.

title: Homer and the Epics Iliad and Odyssey
summary: The epics about the Trojan War and the wanderings of Odysseus are set down in writing.
text: The Iliad and the Odyssey, attributed to the poet Homer, gathered orally transmitted legends about the Trojan War into artful hexameters. They were the foundation of Greek education, shaped the image of the gods and heroes, and were revered as a model from Alexander the Great to the Romans. At the same time the Greeks adopted the Phoenician alphabet and added vowels to it.

title: Delphi and the Oracle of Apollo
summary: The sanctuary of Apollo at Delphi becomes the most important oracle site of the Greek world, consulted by cities and kings before every major decision.
text: On the slope of Mount Parnassus the priestess Pythia, seated on a tripod, proclaimed the answers of the god Apollo, which the priests cast into often ambiguous verse. From the 8th century BC at the latest, poleis sought the advice of Delphi before founding colonies, going to war and reforming their laws, and foreigners too, such as the Lydian king Croesus, sent envoys and votive offerings. The Greek cities erected treasuries there, and from 582 BC the Pythian Games were held, with contests in music and athletics. The maxims Know thyself and Nothing in excess at the temple entrance summed up Greek practical wisdom; Delphi was regarded as the navel of the world and was not closed until AD 391.

title: The Reforms of Solon in Athens
summary: Solon abolishes debt bondage and grants all citizens of Athens political rights according to their wealth.
text: Around 594 BC the poet and statesman Solon was charged with resolving the crisis in Athens, in which indebted farmers had fallen into slavery. He cancelled all debts, forbade the enslavement of citizens for debt, and bought back those who had been carried off. He divided the citizens according to their harvest yield into four classes, which received graduated rights to hold office; even the poorest class was allowed to take part in the assembly and the courts. Solon refused to become a tyrant and left Athens for ten years so that his laws would be put to the test. He is regarded as one of the Seven Sages and as a forerunner of democracy.

title: Cyrus II Founds the Persian Empire
summary: Cyrus defeats the Medes and founds the Achaemenid Empire, the largest empire of its time.
text: Around 550 BC Cyrus II overthrew the Median king Astyages and united Persians and Medes under his rule. In the years that followed he conquered Lydia with its fabulously wealthy king Croesus, and in 539 BC Babylon, where he permitted the deported Jews to return to Jerusalem. His successors extended the empire as far as Egypt and the Indus and administered it through satrapies, royal roads and an imperial postal service.

title: The Tyranny of the Peisistratids in Athens
summary: Peisistratus and his sons rule Athens as tyrants and promote farmers, festivals and the arts, until Hippias is driven out.
text: After two failed attempts, Peisistratus seized lasting power in Athens around 546 BC with the help of mercenaries. He left Solon's laws in force, granted credit to smallholders, had aqueducts and temples built, and staged the Dionysia with its drama competitions and the Panathenaia as great festivals; under him the epics of Homer were set down in writing. After his death in 527 BC his sons Hippias and Hipparchus followed; after the murder of Hipparchus in 514 BC, Hippias ruled harshly until Spartans and Athenian nobles drove him out in 510 BC. The tyrannicides Harmodius and Aristogeiton became heroes of the young democracy.

title: The Beginning of the Roman Republic
summary: The Romans drive out their last king and establish a republic.
text: After the expulsion of King Tarquinius Superbus, two consuls elected annually took over the government. The Senate, the popular assemblies and offices such as praetor, censor and tribune of the plebs formed a system of mutual checks. The Conflict of the Orders between patricians and plebeians led over two centuries to greater rights for the common people, for example through the Law of the Twelve Tables around 450 BC.

title: The Reforms of Cleisthenes and the Beginning of Democracy
summary: Cleisthenes reorganizes the citizenry of Athens and lays the foundation of Athenian democracy.
text: After the fall of the tyranny of the Peisistratids, Cleisthenes divided the citizens of Athens into ten new tribes that mixed city, coast and inland and broke the power of the old aristocratic families. A Council of 500, filled by lot, prepared the decisions of the assembly; ostracism was meant to prevent any individual from grasping too much power. Under Pericles the democracy was later expanded, but it remained restricted to male citizens.

title: The Buddha Teaches in Northern India
summary: Siddhartha Gautama proclaims his teaching on the end of suffering in the Ganges valley.
text: After his enlightenment beneath a fig tree at Bodh Gaya, Siddhartha Gautama gave his first sermon in the deer park at Sarnath on the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path. For about four decades he traveled through northern India as a wandering teacher and founded a community of monks and nuns. His teaching opposed the caste system and the sacrificial priesthood and later became one of the great world religions.

title: Daoism and the Daodejing
summary: In China, Daoism emerges as a teaching of harmony with the Dao, the way of nature.
text: The Daodejing, attributed to the legendary sage Laozi, teaches in 81 short chapters that people should not act against the order of nature but adapt to it. Instead of rules and ceremonies as with Confucius, it recommends restraint, simplicity and non-action, wuwei, for the ruler as well. Daoism later became a popular religion with temples, priests and a search for immortality, and it influenced Chinese medicine, painting and martial arts.

title: Confucius and His Teaching
summary: The scholar Confucius sets out an ethics of humaneness, duty and education.
text: In a time of constant war between the Chinese princely states, Confucius taught that order arises through moral example, respect for parents and rulers, and education. His students collected his sayings in the Analects, the Lunyu. Under the Han dynasty, Confucianism became the state doctrine and remained the basis of Chinese civil service training for more than two thousand years.

title: The Battle of Marathon
summary: The Athenians defeat a Persian landing force and repel the first attack by the Great King Darius.
text: The Persian Great King Darius I sent a fleet to Greece to punish Athens for supporting a revolt in Asia Minor. At Marathon the Athenian hoplites under Miltiades charged the numerically superior Persians at a run and put them to flight. The victory strengthened Athenian self-confidence; the legend of the messenger who ran the news to Athens gave the marathon race its name.

title: The Battle of Thermopylae
summary: King Leonidas and 300 Spartans hold the pass against the Persian army and fall to the last man.
text: When Xerxes marched into Greece in 480 BC with an enormous army, a Greek force of a few thousand men under the Spartan king Leonidas opposed him at the narrow pass of Thermopylae. For two days the Persian attacks broke against the phalanx of the hoplites. When a traitor showed the Persians a mountain path, Leonidas sent most of the allies away and stayed behind with 300 Spartans, 700 Thespians and 400 Thebans, all of whom fell. Militarily a defeat, the battle became a symbol of sacrifice for freedom; the epitaph telling the stranger to report to Sparta that here they lie, obedient to her laws, is famous to this day.

title: The Battle of Salamis
summary: The Greek fleet under Themistocles destroys the Persian fleet of Xerxes in the strait of Salamis.
text: Ten years after Marathon, Xerxes invaded Greece with an enormous army, overcame the Spartans under Leonidas at Thermopylae and destroyed Athens. Themistocles lured the Persian fleet into the narrow bay of Salamis, where the agile Greek triremes defeated the superior force. The following year the Greeks also beat the Persian land army at Plataea; Athens rose to become the leading naval power and founded the Delian League.

title: The Warring States Period and Sunzi's Art of War
summary: Seven Chinese states wage war for two and a half centuries while the philosophers of the Hundred Schools argue over the right order.
text: After the collapse of Zhou rule, the states of Qin, Chu, Qi, Yan, Han, Zhao and Wei fought for supremacy with mass armies of infantry, crossbows and iron weapons. In this crisis, thinkers such as Mencius, Mozi, Zhuangzi and the Legalists sought paths to peace and order; they are known as the Hundred Schools of Thought. The strategist Sunzi set out in The Art of War the principles by which a wise commander wins through deception, planning and knowledge of the enemy, ideally without a battle at all. The era ended in 221 BC with the victory of the state of Qin.

title: Aeschylus and the Flowering of Tragedy
summary: With The Persians by Aeschylus, the oldest surviving tragedy is performed; Athenian theater reaches its height.
text: At the Dionysia, the spring festival of the god Dionysus, three poets competed in Athens each year with three tragedies and a satyr play apiece; performances in the Theater of Dionysus on the slope of the Acropolis drew as many as 15,000 spectators. In 472 BC Aeschylus won with The Persians, which shows the Battle of Salamis from the perspective of the defeated and is the oldest surviving drama in world literature. Aeschylus introduced the second actor and thereby made dialogue possible; Sophocles added the third and wrote Antigone and Oedipus the King, while Euripides portrayed human passion and suffering in Medea and The Trojan Women. Theater was part of political life: the state paid citizens' admission, and the plays worked through questions of law, power and guilt.

title: The Twelve Tables
summary: Rome receives its first written legal code in the Twelve Tables, set up publicly in the Forum.
text: Until the middle of the 5th century BC, only patrician priests and officials knew the law, which left the plebeians exposed to arbitrary treatment. Under their pressure, a commission of ten men, the decemvirs, wrote down the existing law around 450 BC on twelve bronze tables that were set up in the Forum. The provisions governed court procedure, debt, property, family, inheritance and punishment, and some were harsh, for example toward debtors. For the Romans the Twelve Tables remained the origin of their law; schoolchildren still learned them by heart in Cicero's day, and the principle that law must be public and the same for all carried through into modern law.

title: The Height of Athens: Building the Parthenon
summary: Under Pericles the Parthenon rises on the Acropolis, the masterpiece of Greek architecture.
text: After the Persians laid waste to the Acropolis in 480 BC, Pericles pushed through the rebuilding of the temples with the contributions of the Delian League. The architects Ictinus and Callicrates built the Parthenon from 447 to 432 BC out of Pentelic marble, with 46 Doric columns, a 160-meter frieze showing the Panathenaic procession, and inside a twelve-meter statue of Athena in gold and ivory by Phidias. Subtle curves and inclinations of the columns compensate for optical illusions and make the building appear perfect. The temple later became a church and a mosque and was badly damaged by an explosion in 1687; Lord Elgin took a large part of the sculptures to London around 1800, where they remain in the British Museum, still disputed.

title: The Peloponnesian War
summary: Athens and Sparta struggle for almost three decades over supremacy in Greece; Athens loses.
text: The rivalry between the naval power Athens and the land power Sparta led to war in 431 BC, described by the historian Thucydides. A plague carried off Pericles and a large part of the Athenians in 429 BC, and the expedition to Sicily from 415 to 413 BC ended in catastrophe. With Persian money Sparta built a fleet and forced Athens to capitulate in 404 BC; the Greek city-states emerged from the war exhausted.

title: Hippocrates and the Beginnings of Scientific Medicine
summary: On the island of Kos, Hippocrates founds a medicine that traces illness to natural causes.
text: Hippocrates of Kos and his students taught around 420 BC that diseases are not sent by the gods but have natural causes such as climate, diet and way of life. Physicians should observe the sick closely, record the course of the illness and above all do no harm. The roughly 60 writings of the Hippocratic Corpus deal with epidemics, fractures, diet and the doctrine of the four humors, blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile, which shaped medicine into the modern era. The Hippocratic Oath, which binds physicians to confidentiality and to the good of the patient, remains the foundation of medical ethics today.

title: The Trial and Death of Socrates
summary: An Athenian jury court condemns the philosopher Socrates to death by the cup of hemlock.
text: Socrates was charged with not recognizing the gods of the city and with corrupting the youth. Before 500 jurors he defended himself without pleading for mercy and was convicted by a narrow majority. He refused to flee, because he respected the laws of his city, and drank the cup of poison surrounded by his students. Plato made the trial a foundational text of philosophy in his Apology.

title: Alexander's Campaign into Asia
summary: Alexander the Great conquers the Persian Empire in eleven years and pushes as far as India.
text: With about 40,000 men, Alexander crossed the Hellespont in 334 BC, defeated the Persians at the Granicus, at Issus and in 331 BC at Gaugamela, and had himself recognized as pharaoh in Egypt. He marched through Persia and Bactria to the Indus, where his exhausted soldiers forced him to turn back. Alexander founded numerous cities named Alexandria and died in Babylon in 323 BC; his generals, the Diadochi, divided the empire among themselves.

title: The Conquest of Egypt and the Founding of Alexandria
summary: Alexander is recognized as pharaoh in Egypt and founds Alexandria in the Nile Delta, the future capital of the Hellenistic world.
text: After the victory at Issus and the capture of Tyre, Alexander marched into Egypt in 332 BC, where the population received him as a liberator from the Persians and the priests recognized him as pharaoh. At the oasis of Siwa the oracle of Ammon greeted him as the son of the god. In early 331 BC he marked out on the Mediterranean coast west of the Nile Delta the plan of a new city with streets at right angles and two harbors. Under the Ptolemies, Alexandria became the largest city of the Mediterranean world, with its library, its Museion and the lighthouse of Pharos, and it remained a center of trade, scholarship and Greek culture in Egypt into Roman times.

title: The Wars of the Diadochi
summary: Alexander's generals fight over his legacy for four decades until three great kingdoms emerge.
text: Alexander left no capable heir when he died in 323 BC; his generals, the Diadochi, divided the satrapies among themselves and fought one another in shifting alliances. Alexander's mother, his wife Roxana and his son were murdered. Antigonus tried to hold the empire together but fell in 301 BC at the Battle of Ipsus; the wars ended with the Battle of Corupedium in 281 BC. Three great realms remained: that of the Ptolemies in Egypt, of the Seleucids in Syria, Mesopotamia and Iran, and of the Antigonids in Macedon, along with smaller states such as Pergamon. These Hellenistic kingdoms shaped the East until the Roman conquest.

title: The Founding of the Library of Alexandria
summary: The Ptolemies create in Alexandria the largest library and the most important research center of antiquity.
text: Ptolemy I and his son Ptolemy II had a Museion built in Alexandria with an attached library intended to collect hundreds of thousands of scrolls. Scholars such as Euclid, Eratosthenes, who calculated the circumference of the Earth, and Archimedes worked there or were connected with it. Alexandria became the center of Hellenistic scholarship; the library was lost over the following centuries through fires and neglect.

title: The Punic Wars
summary: In three wars Rome wears Carthage down and becomes the leading power in the western Mediterranean.
text: In the First Punic War, Rome gained Sicily and built a large fleet for the first time. In the Second, Hannibal crossed the Alps with elephants and defeated the Romans at Cannae in 216 BC, but lost to Scipio at Zama in 202 BC. The Third Punic War ended in 146 BC with the complete destruction of Carthage.

title: Ashoka and the Spread of Buddhism
summary: After a bloody war, the Maurya king Ashoka turns to Buddhism and proclaims a policy of nonviolence.
text: Ashoka ruled the Maurya Empire, which covered almost the entire Indian subcontinent. By his own account, the suffering of the war against Kalinga around 261 BC moved him to govern thereafter by the principles of Buddhism. On rocks and pillars he had edicts carved about tolerance, welfare and the renunciation of violence, and he sent Buddhist missionaries as far as Sri Lanka and the Hellenistic kingdoms. The lion capital of his pillar at Sarnath is today the state emblem of India.

title: Qin Shi Huang Unifies China and Begins the Great Wall
summary: The king of Qin defeats the last rival states and calls himself First Emperor.
text: After defeating the six remaining Warring States, the king of Qin took the title Shi Huangdi, First August Emperor. He standardized writing, coinage, measures, weights and even the axle width of carts, divided the land into administrative districts, and had existing frontier ramparts joined into a first Great Wall against the mounted nomads in the north. His rule was harsh and rested on the strict doctrine of Legalism; a few years after his death the dynasty fell, but the unified empire endured.

title: Archimedes and the Siege of Syracuse
summary: The war machines of Archimedes hold off the Romans for two years; when the city falls, the scholar is killed.
text: Syracuse, the most powerful Greek city in Sicily, had sided with Carthage in the Second Punic War. When the Roman commander Marcellus besieged the city in 213 BC, catapults, cranes that lifted ships out of the water and other machines designed by Archimedes are said to have repelled the attackers again and again. In 212 BC the Romans broke into the city during a festival. A soldier killed Archimedes, who was reportedly bent over a geometric drawing, against the orders of Marcellus to spare him. Syracuse was plundered and became part of the Roman province of Sicily; the conquest shows how the Greek world came step by step under Roman rule.

title: The Terracotta Army of the First Emperor
summary: Qin Shi Huang is buried in an enormous tomb complex guarded by thousands of life-size clay soldiers.
text: Already as a young king, Qin Shi Huang had begun building his tomb at the foot of Mount Li near Xi'an, on which, according to Sima Qian, as many as 700,000 workers were employed at times. After his death in 210 BC he was laid to rest in an underground palace complex surrounded by pits holding about 8,000 warriors, horses and chariots of fired clay. Each figure has its own face, carried real weapons and was originally painted in color. Farmers discovered the army in 1974 while digging a well; the burial mound itself has still not been opened.

title: Rome Conquers Greece
summary: With the destruction of Corinth, Greece becomes part of the Roman Empire.
text: After victories over Macedon at Cynoscephalae in 197 BC and Pydna in 168 BC, Rome crushed the revolt of the Achaean League in 146 BC and destroyed Corinth. Greece was first placed under the province of Macedonia and later became the province of Achaea. The Romans nevertheless took over Greek art, literature and philosophy; the poet Horace wrote that captive Greece had captured her rough conqueror.

title: The Attempted Reforms of the Gracchi
summary: The tribunes Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus fail with their land reforms and are killed.
text: In 133 BC Tiberius Gracchus wanted to distribute public land to impoverished farmers in order to save the basis of the citizen army. The Senate resisted, Tiberius was beaten to death, and his brother Gaius was driven to his death ten years later. This violence in domestic politics is considered the beginning of the crisis of the Republic.

title: The Han Dynasty and the Silk Road
summary: Under Emperor Wu, China opens trade routes to Central Asia that link the East with the Mediterranean world.
text: Emperor Wu of Han sent the envoy Zhang Qian west to find allies against the mounted nomads of the Xiongnu. His reports on the lands of Central Asia led to regular caravans that carried silk, lacquer and iron westward and brought horses, glass, gold and later Buddhism to China. The Han dynasty ruled from 206 BC to AD 220, raised Confucianism to the state doctrine and established a civil service filled through examinations.

title: Sima Qian Writes the Shiji
summary: The court historian Sima Qian completes the Records of the Grand Historian, the model for all later Chinese histories.
text: Sima Qian continued his father's work and described in 130 chapters the history of China from the mythical Yellow Emperor to his own day under Emperor Wu of Han. He arranged the material into dynastic annals, tables, treatises and biographies, traveled to the places he wrote about and compared his sources critically. When he defended a disgraced general in 99 BC, he was sentenced to castration but chose to go on living in order to finish his work. For two thousand years the Shiji remained the model for the official dynastic histories.

title: The Slave Revolt of Spartacus
summary: The gladiator Spartacus leads tens of thousands of escaped slaves against Roman armies for two years.
text: In 73 BC, Spartacus and about 70 gladiators broke out of a school in Capua and entrenched themselves on Mount Vesuvius. Slaves from the country estates and impoverished farm laborers joined them until the force grew to between 70,000 and 120,000 people and defeated several Roman armies. The march led as far as northern Italy and back south again, where pirates refused the promised passage to Sicily. In 71 BC Marcus Licinius Crassus defeated the rebels in Lucania; Spartacus fell in battle, and 6,000 prisoners were crucified along the Via Appia from Capua to Rome. The revolt was the largest slave war of antiquity and later became a symbol of the fight against oppression.

title: Caesar Conquers Gaul
summary: Gaius Julius Caesar subdues all of Gaul up to the Rhine in eight years.
text: As governor, Caesar waged war against Celtic and Germanic tribes and in 52 BC defeated the uprising under Vercingetorix at Alesia. His accounts, the Gallic War, made him famous in Rome and turned his legions into a power base loyal to him alone. Gaul became a Roman province and was later Romanized.

title: The Assassination of Caesar
summary: On the Ides of March, Caesar is stabbed to death by senators around Brutus and Cassius.
text: After his victory in the civil war against Pompey, Caesar had himself appointed dictator for life. A group of senators feared the end of the Republic and killed him on 15 March 44 BC. Instead of saving the Republic, the deed set off a new civil war at the end of which Octavian stood as sole ruler.

title: The Naval Battle of Actium
summary: Octavian's fleet under Agrippa defeats Mark Antony and Cleopatra and ends the civil wars of the Republic.
text: After Caesar's death, Octavian and Mark Antony had divided the empire between them, but Antony's association with Cleopatra and his grants of eastern territories to her children gave Octavian his pretext for war. On 2 September 31 BC the fleets met off the promontory of Actium on the west coast of Greece. Octavian's admiral Agrippa cut off Antony's heavy ships; Cleopatra and Antony escaped to Egypt with part of the fleet, and their troops surrendered. The following year Octavian took Alexandria, Antony and Cleopatra took their own lives, and Egypt became a Roman province. Actium ended almost a century of civil wars and made Octavian sole ruler.

title: The Death of Cleopatra and the End of the Hellenistic Age
summary: With the suicide of Cleopatra VII, the last Hellenistic kingdom falls to Rome.
text: Cleopatra VII, the last ruler of the Ptolemaic line, had allied herself with Caesar and afterwards with Mark Antony in order to secure Egypt's independence. After the defeat in the naval battle of Actium in 31 BC and Octavian's entry into Alexandria, Antony and Cleopatra took their own lives. Egypt became a Roman province, and with that the age of the Hellenistic kingdoms that had grown out of Alexander's conquests came to an end.

title: Augustus Establishes the Principate
summary: Octavian receives the honorary name Augustus and becomes in effect the first Roman emperor.
text: After his victory over Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BC, Octavian claimed to be restoring the Republic while keeping control of the army, the provinces and the finances. As princeps, first among equals, he ruled for more than forty years and created the foundations of the imperial age. His reign brought internal peace and a cultural golden age with poets such as Virgil and Horace.

title: The Battle of the Teutoburg Forest
summary: Germanic tribes under Arminius destroy three Roman legions.
text: The Cheruscan chieftain Arminius, himself trained in Roman service, lured the governor Varus into an ambush. About 15,000 Romans lost their lives. Rome afterwards abandoned its plans to subdue the territory east of the Rhine for good; the Rhine and later the limes became the frontier.

title: Buddhism Reaches China
summary: Buddhist monks and scriptures reach China along the Silk Road, and the White Horse Temple is founded.
text: According to tradition, Emperor Ming of Han dreamed of a golden figure and sent messengers west, who returned to Luoyang with two Indian monks and sutras carried on a white horse; there the first Buddhist temple in China was built. In fact, traders and monks from Central Asia brought the teaching into the country step by step, and translators such as An Shigao and later Kumarajiva rendered the scriptures into Chinese. In the troubled centuries after the end of the Han, the message of the end of suffering found a wide following; monasteries became landowners, places of learning and lenders.

title: The Eruption of Vesuvius
summary: The volcano buries Pompeii and Herculaneum under ash and preserves them for posterity.
text: Within a few hours the towns on the Bay of Naples were buried under ash, pumice and pyroclastic flows. Thousands of people died, among them the scholar Pliny the Elder. Excavations since the 18th century have given unique insight into everyday life in a Roman town.

title: The Opening of the Colosseum
summary: Emperor Titus inaugurates the largest amphitheater of antiquity with a hundred days of games.
text: From AD 72, Emperor Vespasian had an amphitheater built on the site of the artificial lake of Nero's palace, which his son Titus opened in AD 80 with a hundred days of gladiatorial combat, animal hunts and reportedly a mock naval battle; thousands of animals and many people died in the process. The structure of travertine, brick and concrete held about 50,000 spectators, who sat separated by rank and reached their seats within minutes through 80 numbered entrances; an awning provided shade, and lifts brought animals up from the cellars into the arena. It received the name Colosseum in the Middle Ages, after a colossal statue of Nero nearby. The games allowed the emperor to show himself to the people and prove his generosity; gladiatorial combat took place here until the 5th century.

title: The Kushan Empire Links India to the Silk Road
summary: Under King Kanishka the Kushans rule Central Asia and northern India and promote trade, Buddhism and the art of Gandhara.
text: The Kushans, a people who had migrated from Central Asia, built an empire in the 1st century stretching from the Amu Darya to the Ganges, with capitals at Peshawar and Mathura. It lay at the crossroads of the trade routes between Rome, Persia, India and China and struck gold coins on the Roman model bearing Greek, Persian, Indian and Buddhist deities. Under Kanishka around 130, the first Buddha statues in human form were created in Gandhara, combining Greek and Indian stylistic elements. From here monks and texts of Mahayana Buddhism traveled to Central Asia and China.

title: The Invention of Paper in China
summary: The court official Cai Lun presents the emperor with an improved method of making paper.
text: In the year 105, Cai Lun described a process in which tree bark, hemp, rags and old fishing nets were pounded into a pulp, scooped onto screens and dried. Older paper finds show that simple papers already existed, but now the cheap material replaced bamboo slips and silk. The knowledge reached Japan by way of Korea and, after 751, passed through Arab workshops in Samarkand and Baghdad to reach Europe in the 12th century.

title: The Empire at Its Greatest Extent under Trajan
summary: With the conquest of Dacia, Armenia and Mesopotamia, the Roman Empire reaches its greatest extent under Trajan.
text: Trajan, the first emperor from a province, subdued the Dacian kingdom north of the Danube in two wars from 101 to 106, and its gold mines filled the treasury; Trajan's Column in Rome tells the campaign in a relief band 200 meters long. In 106 the Nabataean kingdom with Petra became the province of Arabia. From 114 Trajan marched against the Parthians, conquered Armenia and Mesopotamia and reached the Persian Gulf, where he is said to have regretted being too old for a campaign to India. At his death in 117 the empire covered about five million square kilometers and more than 60 million people. His successor Hadrian immediately gave up the eastern conquests because they could not be held.

title: The Building of Hadrian's Wall
summary: Emperor Hadrian has a wall 118 kilometers long built across northern Britain as the frontier of the empire.
text: Hadrian broke with the expansionist policy of his predecessor Trajan and secured the frontiers instead. During his visit to Britain in 122 he ordered the construction of a stone wall from the North Sea to the Irish Sea, up to four and a half meters high, with ditches, forts every Roman mile, watchtowers and garrisons in which about 10,000 soldiers from all parts of the empire served. The wall was meant less to repel attacks than to control movement, trade and customs. Wooden tablets from the fort of Vindolanda, with letters, shopping lists and a birthday invitation, give a unique glimpse of everyday life on the frontier. Rome also built fortified frontier lines along the Rhine and the Danube with the limes.

title: Constitutio Antoniniana: Citizenship for All Free Inhabitants
summary: Emperor Caracalla grants Roman citizenship to almost all free inhabitants of the empire.
text: Until 212, only Italians, veterans, elites of the provincial cities and freedmen were Roman citizens, while the majority of provincial inhabitants lived as peregrines under their own law. With an edict partly preserved on a papyrus in Giessen, Caracalla made all free inhabitants of the empire citizens. He gave thanks to the gods as his motive; the historian Cassius Dio suspected that the emperor wanted to extend the inheritance and manumission taxes, paid only by citizens, to everyone. The consequences were far-reaching: Roman law now applied to everyone from Britain to Syria, millions of people took the name Aurelius, and the distinction between conquerors and conquered disappeared.

title: Ardashir I Founds the Sasanian Empire
summary: A Persian prince overthrows the Parthians and builds an empire that is Rome's and Byzantium's great rival for four centuries.
text: Ardashir I of the Sasanian family defeated the last Parthian king in 224 and had himself crowned King of Kings; his capital became Ctesiphon on the Tigris. The Sasanians deliberately linked themselves to the Achaemenids, made Zoroastrianism the state religion and created a tight administration with noble ranks and standing armies of armored cavalry. Shapur I took the Roman emperor Valerian prisoner in 260, and in the 6th century Khosrow I reformed taxation and the army and supported the academy of Gundeshapur. Decades of war with Byzantium exhausted the empire, so that it fell to the Arab conquerors between 636 and 651.

title: The Crisis of the Third Century
summary: For fifty years, soldier emperors, civil wars, plagues, inflation and invasions by Germanic peoples and Persians shake the empire.
text: With the murder of Severus Alexander in 235 began a period in which the legions proclaimed and overthrew more than twenty emperors, hardly one of whom died a natural death. Goths plundered Greece and Asia Minor, Alemanni and Franks pushed into Gaul and Italy, and the Persian king Shapur I captured Emperor Valerian in 260. Gaul and Palmyra under Queen Zenobia broke away for a time as separate empires. The emperors debased the silver coinage until the denarius was almost pure copper, prices multiplied, and cities shrank behind new walls. Aurelian reunited the empire between 270 and 275; only Diocletian ended the crisis in 284 with sweeping reforms.

title: Diocletian Establishes the Tetrarchy
summary: Diocletian divides rule over the empire among four emperors and reforms administration, army and taxation.
text: Diocletian, an officer from Dalmatia, recognized that a single emperor could no longer defend the threatened frontiers everywhere. In 286 he made Maximian co-emperor for the West, and in 293 each of them received a junior emperor, Constantius and Galerius, who were to succeed them. This rule of four governed from residences near the frontiers such as Trier, Milan, Sirmium and Nicomedia. Diocletian doubled the number of provinces, separated civil and military offices, introduced a new tax system and in 301 an edict on maximum prices, and in 303 launched the last great persecution of Christians. In 305 he became the only emperor to abdicate voluntarily and withdrew to his palace in Split; the tetrarchy soon broke apart in civil wars, from which Constantine emerged.

title: The Edict of Milan: Freedom of Religion for Christians
summary: Constantine and Licinius grant the long-persecuted Christians the free practice of their religion.
text: After centuries of intermittent persecution, Christians received full freedom of religion in 313 and the return of their confiscated property. Constantine supported the church, convened the Council of Nicaea in 325 and was baptized on his deathbed. In 380 Emperor Theodosius declared Christianity the state religion.

title: The Gupta Empire as India's Golden Age
summary: Under the Gupta kings, scholarship, literature and art in northern India enjoy a golden age.
text: Chandragupta I founded a dynasty around 320 that under Samudragupta and Chandragupta II ruled most of northern India. The poet Kalidasa worked at the court, the astronomer Aryabhata calculated the circumference of the Earth and the value of pi, and Indian mathematicians developed the place-value system with the digit zero. The cave temples of Ajanta with their wall paintings and classical Sanskrit literature date from this period. In the middle of the 6th century the empire fell apart under the attacks of the Hunas from Central Asia.

title: The Council of Nicaea
summary: At Constantine's invitation, about 300 bishops fix the Christian creed and condemn the teaching of Arius.
text: The dispute between the Alexandrian priest Arius, who regarded Christ as a creature of God and subordinate to him, and his bishop split the church in the East. Constantine, who wanted unity of empire and church, summoned all bishops in 325 to his residence at Nicaea in Asia Minor and took part in the sessions himself. The council declared Christ to be of one substance with the Father, formulated the Nicene Creed that is still spoken in services today, and settled the date of Easter and the ranking of bishops. The Arians were banished, but the dispute went on for decades, and many Germanic peoples adopted Christianity in its Arian form. Nicaea was the first ecumenical council and established the close bond between emperorship and church.

title: The Division of the Roman Empire
summary: After the death of Theodosius, the empire is finally divided into East and West.
text: Theodosius left the West to his son Honorius and the East to his son Arcadius. The Greek-speaking East with Constantinople remained economically strong, while the West fell apart under pressure from Goths, Vandals and Huns. In 410 the Visigoths under Alaric sacked Rome.

title: The Sack of Rome by the Visigoths
summary: The Visigoths under Alaric take Rome and plunder for three days a city no enemy had entered for 800 years.
text: The Visigoths had fled across the Danube into the empire in 376 to escape the Huns and had destroyed a Roman army at Adrianople in 378. Their king Alaric demanded land and offices for his people; when the western court at Ravenna stalled him and had his negotiating partner Stilicho executed, he besieged Rome three times. On 24 August 410 traitors opened the Salarian Gate, and the Goths plundered palaces and temples for three days, though they spared the churches. The news shook the world; Jerome wrote that the city which had conquered the whole world had itself been conquered, and Augustine wrote The City of God in response. Alaric died the same year; the Visigoths later founded a kingdom in southern Gaul and Spain.

title: Attila and the Huns
summary: On the Catalaunian Plains, Romans and Visigoths halt the Hunnic king Attila; his empire falls apart after his death in 453.
text: The Huns, a horse people from the steppes of Asia, had been driving the Goths before them since 375 and thereby set off the Migration Period. Attila, their king from 434, ruled from Hungary an empire stretching from the Baltic to the Black Sea, extorted annual payments of gold from the Eastern Empire and invaded Gaul in 451 with an enormous army. The Roman commander Aetius allied himself with the Visigothic king Theodoric I, who fell in the battle on the Catalaunian Plains near Troyes; Attila had to withdraw. In 452 he laid waste to northern Italy but turned back after a meeting with Pope Leo I. After his sudden death in 453, the Hunnic empire collapsed within a few years, but the Western Empire was so weakened that it lasted only two more decades.

title: The End of the Western Roman Empire
summary: Odoacer deposes Romulus Augustulus, the last Western Roman emperor.
text: The Germanic commander Odoacer sent the imperial insignia to Constantinople and ruled Italy as king. The event is traditionally regarded as the end of antiquity and the beginning of the Middle Ages, even though Roman administration, language and church survived for a long time in the Germanic successor kingdoms.

title: The Baptism of Clovis and the Rise of the Frankish Kingdom
summary: The Frankish king Clovis is baptized a Catholic at Reims and lays the foundation of the leading power in Western Europe.
text: Clovis of the Merovingian line had defeated the last Roman governor in Gaul in 486 and united the Frankish subtribes. Around 498 he was baptized by Bishop Remigius at Reims, reportedly after a vow made in battle against the Alemanni. Because, unlike most Germanic kings, he chose the Catholic rather than the Arian confession, he won the support of the church and of the Roman population. After his victory over the Visigoths in 507 he ruled almost all of Gaul; his kingdom became the nucleus of France and Germany.

title: Benedict of Nursia Founds Monte Cassino
summary: With the monastery of Monte Cassino and his Rule, Benedict founds Western monasticism.
text: Benedict of Nursia had lived as a hermit near Subiaco before founding a monastery around 529 on the mountain of Cassino between Rome and Naples. For his community he wrote a Rule that divided the monks' day between prayer, reading and manual work, demanded moderation and obedience, and made the abbot the father of the community. Over the following centuries the Rule of Benedict prevailed in almost all monasteries of Western Europe. Monasteries such as Monte Cassino, Fulda, St. Gall and Cluny became centers of agriculture, nursing and the art of writing, where ancient manuscripts were preserved.

title: Justinian Consecrates the Hagia Sophia
summary: In Constantinople the largest church in the world is built in just five years, a symbol of the power of the Eastern Roman emperor Justinian.
text: After the Nika riot destroyed the old church in 532, Justinian had the mathematicians Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus build a structure with a seemingly floating dome more than 30 meters across. At the consecration on 27 December 537 he is said to have exclaimed that he had surpassed Solomon. In those same years Justinian had Roman law compiled in the Corpus Iuris Civilis, which shapes the legal order of Europe to this day, and with his generals Belisarius and Narses he reconquered North Africa and Italy. The Hagia Sophia was the largest church in Christendom for almost a thousand years, became a mosque in 1453 and is today a landmark of Istanbul.

title: Muhammad's First Revelation
summary: In a cave on Mount Hira near Mecca, Muhammad receives the first revelation according to Islamic tradition.
text: Muhammad, a merchant of about forty from the Quraysh tribe, regularly withdrew to a cave on Mount Hira to reflect. There, according to Muslim belief, the angel Gabriel appeared to him with the charge to proclaim the words of God. The revelations he received until his death were later collected in the Quran. His preaching of the one God and of responsibility toward the poor and the weak won him his first followers but brought him into conflict with the leading families of Mecca, who profited from the worship of the old gods at the Kaaba.

title: The Beginning of the Tang Dynasty
summary: The Tang dynasty makes China the most powerful and most cosmopolitan empire of its time.
text: Li Yuan founded the Tang dynasty in 618, under which China was a cultural and political great power for almost three centuries. The capital Chang'an, with about a million inhabitants, hosted merchants, monks and envoys from Persia, India, Korea and Japan. The poets Li Bai and Du Fu, woodblock printing and the civil service examinations define the image of this period; in Wu Zetian, the only woman in Chinese history reigned as empress in her own right. After the rebellion of An Lushan from 755, the court gradually lost control of the provinces.

title: The Hijra to Medina
summary: Muhammad and his followers migrate from Mecca to Medina; the Islamic calendar begins with this year.
text: Because of growing hostility in Mecca, Muhammad and his companions accepted an invitation in 622 from the oasis of Yathrib, which from then on was called Medina, the city of the Prophet. There Muhammad became the religious and political head of a community that he bound to the resident tribes in a community charter. After several battles with the Meccans he returned to Mecca in 630 almost without a fight and dedicated the Kaaba to the one God. The caliph Umar later fixed the Hijra as the beginning of the Islamic calendar.

title: The Battle of Badr
summary: The small Muslim community from Medina defeats a considerably larger Meccan army at the oasis of Badr.
text: Two years after the Hijra, in March 624, the first great battle between Muhammad's followers and the leading families of Mecca took place at the oasis of Badr southwest of Medina. About 300 Muslims faced some 1,000 Meccans who had marched out to protect a trade caravan, and nevertheless won a clear victory in which several of their fiercest opponents fell. For the Muslims, Badr was a sign of divine support and considerably strengthened Muhammad's standing in Medina and among the tribes of Arabia. There followed the defeat at Uhud in 625 and the successful defense of Medina at the Battle of the Trench in 627, before Muhammad won Mecca in 630.

title: The Arab Conquest of Jerusalem
summary: The Byzantine city of Jerusalem surrenders to the caliph Umar, who guarantees protection to Christians and Jews.
text: After the victory over the Byzantines at the Yarmuk River in 636, Arab troops besieged Jerusalem, which the patriarch Sophronius handed over personally to the caliph Umar in 638. Umar guaranteed the Christians possession of their churches and once again allowed Jews, after centuries, to settle in the city. On the Temple Mount the Dome of the Rock was later built, completed in 691 and among the oldest Islamic structures. Jerusalem thus became a holy city of all three Abrahamic religions and remained under Muslim rule for more than 450 years.

title: The Umayyad Caliphate in Damascus
summary: Muawiya founds the first caliphal dynasty and makes Damascus the capital of an empire reaching from Spain to the Indus.
text: After the murder of the fourth caliph Ali, the governor of Syria, Muawiya, prevailed and turned the caliphate into a hereditary office of his family. The dispute over the rightful succession to the Prophet led to the split into Sunnis and Shiites that persists to this day. Under the Umayyads, Arab armies conquered North Africa, in 711 the Visigothic kingdom in Spain, and territories as far as Central Asia and the Indus. Arabic became the language of administration, distinct gold coins were minted, and the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus was created as a masterpiece of Islamic architecture.

title: The Battle of Karbala
summary: Husayn, the Prophet's grandson, is killed with his companions by troops of the Umayyad caliph Yazid; the division between Sunnis and Shiites deepens.
text: After the death of the caliph Muawiya in 680, his son Yazid succeeded him, which many Muslims saw as a break with the election of the caliph. Husayn ibn Ali, grandson of Muhammad and son of the fourth caliph Ali, set out with his family and a few dozen companions for Kufa in Iraq, where supporters had invited him to lead them. On 10 October 680 the small group was surrounded at Karbala by a vastly superior army, cut off from the water source and killed after a final fight. For the Shiites, the followers of Ali and his descendants, Husayn became a martyr; they commemorate his death every year on the day of Ashura, and Karbala is one of their most important places of pilgrimage.

title: Wu Zetian Becomes Empress of China
summary: The emperor's former concubine proclaims a dynasty of her own and rules as the only woman in Chinese history to reign in her own right.
text: Wu Zetian was a concubine of two emperors and, after her husband Gaozong fell ill, directed the government from 660; after his death she stripped her sons of power. In 690 she had herself proclaimed emperor, founded the Zhou dynasty and based her rule on Buddhism, which celebrated her as the return of a bodhisattva. She promoted the civil service examinations, brought capable men from simple families into government, and expanded the empire toward Korea and Central Asia. In 705 a palace coup forced her, then over eighty, to abdicate, and the Tang dynasty was restored.

title: The Arab Siege of Constantinople
summary: A large Umayyad army and fleet besiege the Byzantine capital for a year but founder on its walls, on Greek fire and on the winter.
text: After conquering Syria, Egypt and North Africa, the Umayyads wanted to subdue Christian Byzantium as well, whose capital they had already besieged in vain from 674 to 678. In the summer of 717 the commander Maslama encircled Constantinople with a land army and hundreds of ships, and the new emperor Leo III defended it vigorously. Byzantine ships destroyed the Arab fleet with Greek fire, a burning liquid; an unusually harsh winter and epidemics decimated the besiegers, and the Bulgars attacked the Arab camp. In August 718 Maslama broke off the siege; Byzantium endured for another seven centuries and remained the barrier between the caliphate and southeastern Europe.

title: The Battle of Tours and Poitiers
summary: The Frankish mayor of the palace Charles Martel defeats an Arab-Berber army and halts the advance northward.
text: From Spain, Muslim armies repeatedly pushed across the Pyrenees into southern France. In October 732, Charles Martel confronted the governor Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi with his Frankish infantry between Tours and Poitiers; the Arab leader fell and his army withdrew. The significance of the battle was often exaggerated later, but it strengthened the position of the Carolingians, who gained the Frankish crown a few decades afterwards. Muslim rule remained confined to the Iberian Peninsula, where it lasted almost 800 more years.

title: The Abbasid Revolution
summary: A revolt from Khurasan overthrows the Umayyads; the Abbasids take over the caliphate and shift the empire's center eastward.
text: Umayyad rule was hated by many non-Arab Muslims, above all Persians, because despite their conversion to Islam they paid higher taxes and remained excluded from office; the Shiites and many pious Arabs rejected the dynasty as well. The Abbasids, descendants of an uncle of the Prophet, gathered these discontented groups, and in 747 troops rose under the commander Abu Muslim in Khurasan beneath black banners.
