In January 750 they defeated the Umayyad army at the Great Zab in Iraq, the last Umayyad caliph Marwan II was killed while fleeing in Egypt, and almost the entire family fell victim to a massacre. Only Abd al-Rahman escaped to Spain, where he founded the Emirate of Córdoba in 756. The Abbasids opened administration and court to Persians and other peoples and, with Baghdad, made Iraq the center of the Islamic world.

title: The Founding of Baghdad
summary: The Abbasid caliph al-Mansur founds a new capital on the Tigris that becomes the largest city in the world.
text: After the Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads in 750, the caliph al-Mansur had a circular royal city built on the Tigris, which he called Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace. Its favorable position on the trade routes between Persia, India, Arabia and the Mediterranean made Baghdad grow quickly; by around 900 more than half a million people probably lived there. Markets, libraries, hospitals and mosques made the city the center of the Islamic world. The tales of the Thousand and One Nights reflect the splendor of Abbasid Baghdad.

title: The Raid on Lindisfarne: the Beginning of the Viking Age
summary: Scandinavian seafarers plunder the monastery of Lindisfarne off the English coast and cause horror across Europe.
text: On 8 June 793, Vikings landed on the island of Lindisfarne, killed monks, stole church treasures and carried off captives. The attack is regarded as the beginning of the Viking Age, in which Northmen with their fast longships raided coasts and rivers from England to the Mediterranean. They were at the same time traders, explorers and settlers: they founded Dublin and Normandy, controlled trade routes to Russia and Byzantium, and around 1000 reached Iceland, Greenland and North America.

title: The Heian Period in Japan
summary: With the move of the capital to Heian-kyo, today's Kyoto, the classical court culture of Japan begins.
text: Emperor Kanmu moved the court to Heian-kyo in 794 to escape the influence of the powerful Buddhist monasteries of Nara. The noble Fujiwara family effectively governed in place of the emperors for centuries. At court the Japanese syllabaries were created, along with works such as The Tale of Genji by the lady-in-waiting Murasaki Shikibu, regarded as the first novel in world literature. When the warrior families of the Minamoto and the Taira fought for power, the era ended in 1185 with the establishment of the first shogunate.

title: The Imperial Coronation of Charlemagne
summary: Pope Leo III crowns the Frankish king emperor in Rome on Christmas Day and renews the Western empire.
text: Charlemagne had built the Frankish kingdom through wars against Lombards, Saxons and Avars into the largest realm in Western Europe since Rome. When he protected Pope Leo III against his Roman opponents, the pope placed the imperial crown on his head in St. Peter's on 25 December 800. With that the West again claimed an empire of its own alongside Byzantium. Charlemagne reorganized administration, coinage and church, had schools founded and a new, easily legible script developed; this is known as the Carolingian Renaissance.

title: Al-Khwarizmi Founds Algebra
summary: The mathematician al-Khwarizmi writes a textbook in Baghdad on solving equations, from whose title the word algebra comes.
text: Around 820, Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi wrote at the court of the caliph al-Mamun The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing, in Arabic al-jabr wa'l-muqabala. In it he showed step by step how equations of the first and second degree can be solved, and explained their application to inheritance division, trade and land surveying; from al-jabr came the word algebra. In a second work he explained calculation with the Indian numerals and zero, which spread through Europe in Latin translation under his name as algorismus; from this came the term algorithm. Al-Khwarizmi also calculated astronomical tables and wrote a work of geography with the coordinates of more than 2,000 places.

title: The House of Wisdom in Baghdad
summary: Under the caliph al-Mamun, Baghdad becomes a center of translation and scholarship.
text: Harun al-Rashid had already built up a library in Baghdad; his son al-Mamun expanded it into an academy in which scholars translated Greek, Persian and Indian writings into Arabic. The mathematician al-Khwarizmi wrote his textbook on calculating with equations here, from whose title the word algebra and from whose name the term algorithm arose. Astronomers measured the circumference of the Earth, and physicians such as Hunayn ibn Ishaq translated Galen and Hippocrates. The numerals with zero taken over from India spread from here throughout the Islamic world and later to Europe.

title: The Treaty of Verdun
summary: The grandsons of Charlemagne divide the Frankish empire into three parts; from West and East Francia, France and Germany emerge.
text: After the death of Louis the Pious in 840, his sons fought over the inheritance until they agreed on a partition at Verdun in 843: Charles the Bald received the west, Louis the German the east, and Lothair I, who held the imperial title, an elongated middle kingdom stretching from the North Sea to Italy. The year before, Charles and Louis had sworn their alliance in the Oaths of Strasbourg in Old French and Old High German, the oldest surviving texts in either language. The middle kingdom soon broke apart and remained a bone of contention between its neighbors into the 20th century, while the East and West Frankish kingdoms developed into Germany and France.

title: The Diamond Sutra: the oldest dated printed book
summary: A Buddhist text is printed from woodblocks in China; it is still regarded as the oldest dated printed work in the world.
text: The Diamond Sutra is a scroll five meters long, made of seven sheets pasted together, whose closing note records that a certain Wang Jie had it made on 11 May 868 in memory of his parents. Text and a frontispiece were cut in mirror image into wooden blocks, inked, and pressed onto paper; the technique had been in use in China since the 7th century for amulets and calendars. The scroll lay for more than a thousand years in a walled-up cave near Dunhuang, until the explorer Aurel Stein acquired it in 1907; today it is kept in the British Library. In the 11th century Bi Sheng in China also invented movable type made of clay.

title: Caliphate of Córdoba
summary: Abd al-Rahman III proclaims himself caliph in Spain and makes Córdoba the most splendid city in Europe.
text: After the fall of the Umayyads in Damascus, a fugitive of the dynasty had founded an emirate of his own in Spain. In 929 Abd al-Rahman III assumed the title of caliph, placing himself on a par with the Abbasids in Baghdad and the Fatimids in North Africa. Córdoba had paved and lighted streets, baths, hundreds of mosques, and a library said to hold 400,000 volumes; in the palace city of Madinat al-Zahra the caliph received envoys from Byzantium and the Frankish empire. Muslims, Jews, and Christians long lived together in al-Andalus in relative peace. In 1031 the caliphate broke apart into numerous small kingdoms.

title: Otto I triumphs at the Lechfeld
summary: The East Frankish king defeats the Hungarians near Augsburg and is crowned emperor seven years later.
text: Since the end of the 9th century, mounted Hungarian warriors had plundered central Europe almost every year. When they besieged Augsburg in 955, which Bishop Ulrich was defending, Otto I led an army drawn from all the tribes of the realm against them on 10 August and won a complete victory at the Lechfeld. The Hungarians then settled permanently in the Pannonian plain and adopted Christianity around 1000. Otto's standing was now so great that Pope John XII crowned him emperor in Rome in 962; this was the beginning of the Holy Roman Empire, which lasted until 1806.

title: The Fatimids found Cairo and al-Azhar
summary: The Shiite Fatimids conquer Egypt, found the royal city of al-Qahira, and build the al-Azhar mosque as a place of learning.
text: The Fatimids, a Shiite dynasty that traced its descent from Fatima, the daughter of the Prophet, had established a caliphate of their own in North Africa in 909. In 969 their general Jawhar conquered Egypt and had a new palace city laid out north of the old capital Fustat, which was given the name al-Qahira, the victorious; from this came Cairo. From 970 the al-Azhar mosque was built there, where jurists and theologians soon taught; it is regarded as one of the oldest universities still in existence. Under the Fatimids, Cairo became the richest center of the Islamic world, with libraries, markets, and trade across the Red Sea to India; after the dynasty ended in 1171, Saladin made al-Azhar a Sunni institution of learning, which it remains to this day.

title: Rise of the Chola empire in South India
summary: Under Rajaraja I and Rajendra I, the Cholas become the leading land and sea power of the Indian Ocean.
text: Rajaraja I ascended the Chola throne in the Tamil south of India in 985, subdued the neighboring kingdoms and Sri Lanka, and had the enormous Brihadishvara temple to Shiva built at Thanjavur. His son Rajendra I sent an army as far as the Ganges and, in 1025, a fleet against the kingdom of Srivijaya on Sumatra in order to control the sea routes to China. The Cholas governed their empire through village assemblies whose decisions are recorded in temple inscriptions, and their bronze sculptors created the dancing Shiva Nataraja, a masterpiece of world art. The empire broke apart in the 13th century.

title: Christianization of Kievan Rus
summary: Grand Prince Vladimir is baptized and makes Orthodox Christianity the religion of his realm on the Dnieper.
text: Kievan Rus had emerged in the 9th century from Scandinavian merchant-warriors, the Varangians, and Slavic tribes, and it controlled the trade route from the Baltic to Byzantium. Vladimir I was baptized in 988, married Anna, the sister of the Byzantine emperor Basil II, and had the population of Kiev baptized in the Dnieper. With the faith came the Cyrillic script, canon law, icon painting, and master builders from Byzantium; under Yaroslav the Wise the Cathedral of Saint Sophia in Kiev and the first law code were created. Rus thus became the cradle of Russian, Ukrainian, and Belarusian culture, until the Mongols destroyed Kiev in 1240.

title: Murasaki Shikibu completes The Tale of Genji
summary: At the Japanese imperial court, a lady-in-waiting writes the story of Prince Genji, regarded as the first novel in world literature.
text: Murasaki Shikibu served Empress Shoshi at the court of Heian-kyo, where she wrote the story of Prince Genji, his love affairs, and his descendants in 54 chapters, using the Japanese syllabary. Her diary mentions the work for the first time in 1008, when parts of it were already being read aloud at court. With a fine feeling for emotion, the seasons, and transience, the novel depicts the courtly world of the Heian period, and in Japan it was copied, illustrated, and annotated for centuries. At the same time her rival Sei Shonagon wrote The Pillow Book, a collection of observations and lists.

title: The Song dynasty: gunpowder, compass, and paper money
summary: The first recipe for gunpowder is recorded in Song China in 1044; the compass, paper money, and movable type follow in the same century.
text: The Song dynasty, founded in 960, ruled an economically flourishing China with cities of a million people such as Kaifeng and Hangzhou. In 1044 the military manual Wujing Zongyao described for the first time mixtures of saltpeter, sulfur, and charcoal for fire arrows and bombs; fire lances and explosive bombs followed in the 12th century. In 1088 the scholar Shen Kuo recorded how a magnetized needle points south, and Chinese seafarers soon used the compass for navigation. The state issued the world's first paper money, Bi Sheng invented movable type, and iron production reached quantities that Europe did not match again until the 18th century.

title: Battle of Hastings
summary: Duke William of Normandy defeats the Anglo-Saxon king Harold and conquers England.
text: After the death of the childless king Edward the Confessor, William claimed the English throne, which Harold Godwinson had, however, already taken. On 14 October 1066 the armies met near Hastings; Harold fell in the fighting, and William had himself crowned at Westminster at Christmas. The Norman Conquest brought to England a French-speaking nobility, castles of stone, the feudal system, and a tight administration, recorded in the Domesday Book of 1086. The Bayeux Tapestry tells the events across seventy meters of cloth.

title: The Seljuks win at Manzikert
summary: Sultan Alp Arslan defeats the Byzantine army and takes Emperor Romanos IV prisoner; Anatolia becomes Turkish and Islamic.
text: The Seljuks, a Turkic nomadic people from Central Asia, had adopted Sunni Islam, taken Baghdad in 1055, and placed the Abbasid caliph under their protection; from then on their ruler bore the title of sultan. On 26 August 1071 Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes faced Alp Arslan's army at Manzikert in eastern Anatolia, was defeated by the cavalry tactics of the Turks, and was taken captive. Alp Arslan released him for a ransom, but civil wars broke out in Byzantium, and Turkish tribes advanced almost unhindered into Asia Minor, where the Sultanate of Rum arose with its capital at Konya. The Byzantine emperor's appeal to the pope for help was one of the reasons for the First Crusade in 1096.

title: The Investiture Controversy and the road to Canossa
summary: King Henry IV stands as a penitent before the castle of Canossa and asks Pope Gregory VII to lift his excommunication.
text: Pope Gregory VII had forbidden rulers to install bishops in office with ring and staff, because he wanted to free the church from secular power. When Henry IV responded in 1076 by declaring the pope deposed, Gregory pronounced the ban on the king and released his subjects from their oath of loyalty. Pressed by the princes, Henry crossed the Alps in winter and waited for three days in January 1077 in penitential dress before the castle of Canossa, until Gregory received him back into the church. The conflict continued for decades and was ended only in 1122 by a compromise in the Concordat of Worms.

title: Founding of the University of Bologna
summary: Europe's first university grows out of the law schools of Bologna; Paris and Oxford follow in the 12th century.
text: In Bologna scholars such as Irnerius had specialized in the rediscovered Roman law of Justinian and attracted students from all over Europe. Around 1088 these students joined together in corporations that hired professors and regulated teaching; the word university originally denoted this community of teachers and learners. Emperor Frederick Barbarossa placed the scholars under his protection in 1155, and the popes gave their degrees validity throughout Christendom. By 1500 there were around 70 universities, among them Paris, Oxford, Salamanca, Prague, Vienna, and Heidelberg.

title: The First Crusade and the capture of Jerusalem
summary: At the pope's call, knights from all over Europe march to the Holy Land and capture Jerusalem.
text: At the Synod of Clermont in 1095, Pope Urban II called for help for the Byzantine Christians and for the liberation of the holy sites from Muslim rule. Tens of thousands answered the call, among them knights under Godfrey of Bouillon and Raymond of Toulouse. After a costly march through Asia Minor and the siege of Antioch, the crusaders took Jerusalem on 15 July 1099 and carried out a massacre of the population. They founded several crusader states, which held out for almost two centuries; six more major crusades followed.

title: The beginning of Gothic architecture at Saint-Denis
summary: Abbot Suger has a light-filled choir built near Paris and with it establishes the style of the Gothic cathedrals.
text: In 1140 Abbot Suger began rebuilding the abbey church of Saint-Denis, the burial place of the French kings, combining pointed arches, ribbed vaults, and large stained-glass windows into a new whole. Because the weight of the vaults was carried from outside by buttresses, the walls could be made thin and the light, which for Suger was an image of God, could enter unhindered. Within a few decades the cathedrals of Chartres, Paris, Reims, and Amiens were built on this model, and in 1248 construction of Cologne Cathedral began. With their towers, sculptures, and rose windows, the Gothic cathedrals were the tallest buildings of their time and an expression of the pride of the growing cities.

title: Construction of Angkor Wat
summary: The Khmer build the largest temple complex in the world in present-day Cambodia.
text: In the first half of the 12th century, King Suryavarman II had Angkor Wat built as a temple to the Hindu god Vishnu and as his own tomb. Surrounded by moats, the complex with its five towers reproduces Mount Meru, the world mountain of Hindu cosmology, and is decorated with reliefs kilometers long. The Khmer empire then ruled large parts of Southeast Asia and supplied its capital by means of an ingenious canal system. Angkor Wat later became a Buddhist sanctuary and is today the national symbol of Cambodia.

title: Ibn Rushd explains Aristotle in Córdoba
summary: At the request of the Almohad caliph, the judge and physician Ibn Rushd begins his commentaries on Aristotle, which change the thought of Europe.
text: Around 1169 the Almohad caliph Abu Yaqub Yusuf commissioned the scholar Ibn Rushd of Córdoba to explain the difficult writings of Aristotle. Over the following decades Ibn Rushd wrote commentaries on almost all the works of the Greek philosopher and, in a treatise of his own, defended the compatibility of reason and revelation against the criticism of the theologian al-Ghazali. In 1195 he fell out of favor for a time because of his philosophy and had to go into exile. His commentaries were translated into Latin and Hebrew as early as the 13th century; at the University of Paris he was known simply as the Commentator, and Thomas Aquinas engaged with him intensively.

title: Saladin retakes Jerusalem
summary: After his victory at Hattin, Saladin takes the city again almost nine decades after the First Crusade.
text: Saladin had united Egypt and Syria under his rule and called for war against the crusader states. On 4 July 1187, at the Horns of Hattin, he destroyed the army of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, which was cut off from water in the summer heat. On 2 October Jerusalem capitulated; unlike the crusaders in 1099, Saladin spared the inhabitants and let them leave on payment of a ransom. The loss of the city set off the Third Crusade, in which Richard the Lionheart did win back Acre, but Jerusalem remained in Muslim hands.

title: The flourishing of Great Zimbabwe
summary: In southern Africa the ancestors of the Shona build a stone city that lives from the gold trade with the Swahili coast.
text: Between the 11th and 15th centuries a city of up to 18,000 inhabitants arose on the plateau of present-day Zimbabwe, its rulers controlling cattle herds and gold deposits. Its walls of carefully layered granite blocks, set without mortar, reach eleven meters in height; the Great Enclosure with its conical tower is the largest precolonial structure south of the Sahara. Finds of Chinese porcelain, Persian ceramics, and Arab coins show that gold and ivory were traded through ports such as Kilwa and Sofala as far as India and China. The city was abandoned around 1450; colonial researchers long disputed the African origin of the buildings, which today give the state of Zimbabwe its name and its emblem.

title: Genghis Khan unites the Mongols
summary: Temüjin is proclaimed ruler of all the Mongol tribes and begins to build a world empire.
text: At an assembly of the tribes on the Onon River in 1206, Temüjin received the title Genghis Khan, which means roughly oceanic or universal ruler. He organized the Mongols into units of ten, a hundred, and a thousand warriors, introduced a law code, and promoted men by achievement rather than by birth. His mounted archers conquered northern China, Central Asia, and Persia; his successors extended the empire as far as Eastern Europe and southern China. Despite the brutality of their warfare, the Pax Mongolica later secured trade along the Silk Road.

title: Magna Carta
summary: English barons force King John to acknowledge their rights in a charter.
text: King John Lackland had turned the nobility against him through lost wars in France and heavy levies. On 15 June 1215, in the meadow of Runnymede, he had to set his seal to Magna Carta, which laid down among other things that no free man may be imprisoned without lawful judgment and that no tax may be levied without the consent of the council. The charter at first applied only to the nobility and was soon annulled again, yet it was confirmed over and over and became a symbol of the ruler's subjection to the law.

title: The Mongols destroy Baghdad
summary: Hülegü's army captures and plunders Baghdad and brings the Abbasid caliphate to an end.
text: The Mongol prince Hülegü, a grandson of Genghis Khan, marched on Baghdad with an enormous army after its caliph al-Mustasim had refused to submit. After a short siege the city fell in February 1258; tens of thousands of inhabitants were killed, palaces, mosques, and libraries were destroyed, and the caliph was executed. The end of the Abbasid caliphate and the devastation of the irrigation system in Mesopotamia struck the Islamic world hard. In 1260 the Mamluks of Egypt halted the Mongol advance at Ain Jalut in Palestine; a few decades later the Mongol rulers of Persia themselves adopted Islam.

title: Marco Polo's journey to China
summary: The young Venetian travels with his father and uncle along the Silk Road to the court of the Mongol ruler Kublai Khan.
text: In 1271 the seventeen-year-old Marco Polo set out from Venice with his father Niccolò and his uncle Maffeo, and after almost four years reached the residence of Kublai Khan in China. By his own account he spent some seventeen years in the service of the Great Khan and traveled through large parts of East Asia before returning by sea in 1295. In Genoese captivity he dictated his experiences, which became known as Il Milione. The account of paper money, coal, and huge cities shaped the European picture of Asia and later inspired Columbus.

title: Founding of the Ottoman Empire
summary: The Turkish prince Osman makes himself independent in northwestern Anatolia and founds a dynasty that will rule for six centuries.
text: After the collapse of the Sultanate of Rum, numerous Turkish principalities arose in Anatolia. On the border with Byzantium, Osman I led warriors who saw themselves as fighters for the faith, and step by step he conquered Byzantine cities. His son Orhan took Bursa in 1326 and made it the first capital; in 1354 the Ottomans crossed into Europe. Within 150 years they had conquered the Balkans and Constantinople and had become the leading power of the Islamic world, one that lasted until 1922.

title: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca
summary: The king of the Mali empire crosses the Sahara to Mecca with an enormous caravan and tons of gold.
text: Mansa Musa ruled the Mali empire, which with the gold mines of the western Sudan and the trading cities of Timbuktu and Gao was among the richest states in the world. On his pilgrimage in 1324 he was accompanied, according to contemporary reports, by thousands of people and camels loaded with gold, which he gave away so freely in Cairo that the price of gold there fell for years. On the way back he brought scholars and master builders with him and had mosques and schools built in Timbuktu. The Catalan Atlas of 1375 shows him holding a nugget of gold as the ruler of West Africa.

title: The travels of Ibn Battuta
summary: A Moroccan jurist crosses the entire Islamic world from West Africa to China in almost thirty years.
text: Ibn Battuta set out from Tangier in 1325 on the pilgrimage to Mecca and then traveled on: to East Africa, Anatolia, the court of the Golden Horde, and India, where he served for years as a judge to the sultan of Delhi, and on to the Maldives, Sumatra, and China. After his return he also visited al-Andalus and the Mali empire in West Africa. In all he covered around 120,000 kilometers, far more than Marco Polo. His travel account, the Rihla, is one of the most important sources on society, trade, and everyday life in the Islamic world of the 14th century.

title: Founding of Tenochtitlan by the Aztecs
summary: The Mexica found the city that becomes the capital of the Aztec empire on an island in Lake Texcoco.
text: According to tradition, the Mexica settled where they saw an eagle on a cactus, as their god Huitzilopochtli had foretold; that image adorns the flag of Mexico today. Through causeways, floating gardens, and canals, the island settlement grew into a city of more than 200,000 inhabitants, with huge temple pyramids and markets. From 1428 Tenochtitlan, in a triple alliance with Texcoco and Tlacopan, ruled large parts of Central America and demanded tribute and captives for human sacrifice. In 1521 the Spaniards under Cortés conquered the city; Mexico City arose on its ruins.

title: Timbuktu becomes a center of trade and scholarship
summary: Under the Mali empire, the caravan city on the Niger develops into a center of the gold trade and of Islamic scholarship.
text: Timbuktu had come into being around 1100 as a camping place of Tuareg nomads on the edge of the Sahara, where caravans carrying salt from the desert met boats from the Niger carrying gold, ivory, and slaves. After his pilgrimage to Mecca, Mansa Musa brought back the Andalusian architect Abu Ishaq al-Sahili in 1325, who built the great Djinguereber Mosque out of mud brick; at the Sankoré Mosque and in private houses, schools arose in which scholars from North Africa and Egypt taught law, grammar, astronomy, and medicine. In the 15th and 16th centuries, under the Songhai empire, Timbuktu was one of the most important centers of learning in Africa, with thousands of students and a lively trade in manuscripts. Tens of thousands of these manuscripts survive to this day and refute the prejudice that Africa south of the Sahara had no written culture.

title: The Hundred Years' War
summary: England and France struggle for more than a century over the French throne and the territories in western France.
text: The war began when the English king Edward III, as the grandson of a French king, claimed the crown of France. English longbowmen won at Crécy in 1346, Poitiers in 1356, and Agincourt in 1415, and for a time France was close to falling apart. In 1429 Joan of Arc turned the tide by relieving Orléans and led the Dauphin to his coronation at Reims. With the battle of Castillon in 1453, England lost all its possessions on the mainland except Calais; both countries emerged from the war with a stronger sense of nationhood and with standing armies.

title: The Black Death
summary: The plague spreads along trade routes across the whole of Europe and kills about a third of the population.
text: In the autumn of 1347 Genoese ships from the Crimea brought the plague to Messina, from where it spread within four years across Italy, France, England, Germany, and Scandinavia. The pathogen Yersinia pestis was transmitted by fleas from rats and was incurable; whole villages died out. Many looked for someone to blame and murdered Jews in numerous cities. The catastrophe led to a shortage of labor, rising wages, peasant revolts, and a new view of death and transience in art and religion.

title: The heyday of the Alhambra in Granada
summary: The Nasrid sultans build the Alhambra palace city in Granada, the most magnificent structure of Islamic Spain.
text: After the Christian kingdoms had conquered Córdoba and Seville in the 13th century, the Emirate of Granada remained as the last Muslim state on the Iberian Peninsula and paid tribute to Castile. On a hill above the city, the Nasrid sultans expanded the Alhambra, the red fortress, into a fortified palace city; its finest parts, such as the Comares Palace and the Court of the Lions, were built around the middle of the 14th century under Yusuf I and Muhammad V. Stucco ornament, calligraphy with verses from the Quran and with poems, colored tiles, wooden ceilings, and gardens threaded with water make the complex a high point of Islamic art. After 1492 the Spanish monarchs continued to use the Alhambra, so that it survived almost unchanged and today belongs to the World Heritage.

title: First Hanseatic Diet in Lübeck
summary: The merchants and cities of the Hanseatic League meet for the first time in a joint assembly and become the trading power of the north.
text: From the 12th century onward, Low German merchants had joined together in associations in order to obtain protection and privileges abroad; trading posts in London, Bruges, Bergen, and Novgorod were their bases. In 1356 the representatives of the cities gathered for the first time in Lübeck for a Hanseatic Diet, which passed joint resolutions on trade, law, and war. At its height some 200 cities from Cologne to Reval belonged to the League, which in the Peace of Stralsund in 1370 even forced the king of Denmark into far-reaching concessions. With the rise of the Dutch and of the territorial princes, the League lost importance in the 16th century; the last Hanseatic Diet was held in 1669.

title: The conquests of Timur
summary: From Samarkand, Timur subdues Persia, India, Syria, and Anatolia and makes his capital a center of art and learning.
text: Timur, a Turco-Mongol warlord from what is now Uzbekistan, seized power in Samarkand in 1370 and waged war almost without interruption for the next 35 years. His mounted armies conquered Persia, defeated the Golden Horde in 1395, plundered Delhi in 1398 and Aleppo, Damascus, and Baghdad in 1400 and 1401, and in 1402 defeated the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I near Ankara, who died in captivity. As a warning Timur had towers built out of skulls; hundreds of thousands died in his campaigns, and whole regions were laid waste. At the same time he brought craftsmen, master builders, and scholars to Samarkand, where splendid mosques and mausoleums were built and where his grandson Ulugh Beg later erected one of the best observatories in the world. Timur died in 1405 at the start of a campaign against China; his descendant Babur founded the Mughal empire in India in 1526.

title: The Peasants' Revolt in England
summary: Tens of thousands of peasants and craftsmen march on London under Wat Tyler and demand the end of serfdom.
text: After the Black Death, wage laborers had gained more bargaining power, but laws froze wages, and a poll tax for the war against France hit poor and rich equally hard. In June 1381 the counties of Kent and Essex rose up, marched on London under the leadership of Wat Tyler, opened prisons, and killed the Archbishop of Canterbury. The preacher John Ball asked where the nobleman had been when Adam delved and Eve span. The fourteen-year-old king Richard II promised the abolition of serfdom, but after Tyler was struck down during the negotiations the revolt was put down; serfdom nevertheless largely disappeared in England over the following decades.

title: Brunelleschi completes the dome of Florence Cathedral
summary: Filippo Brunelleschi completes the huge dome of Santa Maria del Fiore, the emblem of the early Renaissance.
text: Work on the cathedral of Florence had been going on since 1296, but no one knew how the opening, more than 40 meters wide, could be vaulted over. In 1420 Brunelleschi designed a double-shelled dome that was built without wooden centering, and for it he invented hoisting machines and a herringbone pattern of brickwork. On 25 March 1436 Pope Eugene IV consecrated the cathedral; the dome remained the largest masonry dome in the world into the 20th century and proved that the builders of the present could surpass antiquity.

title: Pachacuti builds up the Inca empire
summary: An Inca ruler turns the small kingdom of Cusco into a great empire that soon stretches across the whole of the Andes.
text: Around 1438 the prince Cusi Yupanqui repelled an attack by the Chanka on Cusco, dethroned his father, and took the name Pachacuti, he who overturns the world. In a good three decades he subdued the peoples of the highlands, had Cusco laid out anew as the capital, and introduced storehouses, labor service, and administration by means of knotted cords, the quipus. The mountain city of Machu Picchu was probably built under him as well. His successors extended the empire of the four parts, Tawantinsuyu, from Ecuador to Chile; with around ten million inhabitants it was the largest empire in the Americas when the Spaniards arrived in 1532.

title: Gutenberg invents printing with movable type
summary: In Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg develops a printing process using movable metal type and a printing press.
text: Gutenberg combined cast individual letters made of a lead alloy, a printing press modeled on the wine press, and an oil-based printing ink. Around 1454 he completed the forty-two-line Bible, the first great printed book of Europe. Within fifty years printing shops had been set up in more than 250 European cities, and books became affordable for many people.

title: The fall of Constantinople
summary: The Ottomans under Mehmed II capture the Byzantine capital and bring the Eastern Roman Empire to an end.
text: After almost two months of siege, Ottoman troops broke through the walls of Constantinople on 29 May 1453 with the help of enormous cannon; the last emperor, Constantine XI, fell in the fighting. Sultan Mehmed II made the city, under the name Istanbul, the capital of his empire and had the Hagia Sophia converted into a mosque. Many regard the event as the end of the Middle Ages: Greek scholars fled to Italy and fostered the Renaissance there, and the search for new trade routes to Asia accelerated the European voyages of exploration.

title: The fall of Granada
summary: The last emir of Granada hands the city over to Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon; Muslim rule in Spain ends after almost 800 years.
text: From 1482 the Catholic Monarchs Isabella and Ferdinand waged war against the Emirate of Granada, weakened by family strife, and took city after city. After a siege lasting months, Emir Muhammad XII, whom the Spaniards called Boabdil, handed over the Alhambra on 2 January 1492; according to legend he wept at his last sight of the city. The treaty of surrender guaranteed the Muslims freedom of religion and their property, yet as early as around 1500 they were forced to be baptized, and from 1609 to 1614 Spain expelled the descendants of these Moriscos. In that same year, 1492, the Jews had to leave Spain, and Columbus sailed west on the monarchs' commission. With Granada the Reconquista came to an end, the reconquest of the peninsula by the Christian kingdoms, which had begun in 711 with the Arab conquest.

title: Columbus reaches America
summary: In search of a sea route to India, Christopher Columbus lands on an island in the Bahamas on 12 October 1492.
text: With three ships Columbus had sailed west from Palos on the commission of the Spanish crown, because he believed the earth to be smaller than it is. Until his death he believed that he had reached the east coast of Asia. In fact his landing began the lasting contact between Europe and America, which fundamentally changed the history of both continents.

title: Askia Mohammed takes power in the Songhai empire
summary: With Askia Mohammed begins the golden age of the Songhai empire, the largest state in West Africa, with Timbuktu as a center of scholarship.
text: After the death of the conqueror Sunni Ali, the general Mohammed Ture overthrew his son and took the ruler's title of Askia. He reorganized the empire on the Niger with provinces, officials, and a professional army, made the pilgrimage to Mecca in 1496, and promoted Islam as a unifying religion. Timbuktu with its Sankoré Mosque, and Djenné, became centers of Islamic scholarship whose manuscripts survive to this day. Trade in gold, salt, and slaves across the Sahara made Songhai one of the richest powers of the age; in 1591 it was shattered by Moroccan troops with firearms.

title: Treaty of Tordesillas
summary: Spain and Portugal divide the newly discovered lands of the world, and those still to be discovered, between them along a line in the Atlantic.
text: After the return of Columbus, the two sea powers quarreled over the rights to the new lands, and in 1493 Pope Alexander VI proposed a dividing line. In the treaty of 7 June 1494 it was fixed 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands: everything west of it was to belong to Spain, everything east of it to Portugal. Brazil, reached in 1500, thus fell to Portugal, which is still evident today in the language of the country. Other powers such as England and France never recognized the division; the treaty shows how matter-of-factly European rulers disposed of foreign continents.

title: Vasco da Gama reaches India
summary: The Portuguese Vasco da Gama sails around Africa and is the first European to reach India by sea.
text: After a voyage of almost a year around the Cape of Good Hope, da Gama landed at Calicut on the Malabar Coast of India in May 1498. The new sea route bypassed the Arab and Venetian middlemen and made Portugal the leading power in the spice trade for a century. Portuguese bases were soon established from East Africa as far as China and Japan.

title: Michelangelo completes the David
summary: Michelangelo's marble statue of David, more than five meters high, is set up in Florence.
text: Michelangelo Buonarroti created the figure from a block of marble on which other sculptors had previously tried their hand in vain. The statue shows the biblical hero in tense stillness before the fight and became a symbol of the free republic of Florence. It is regarded as a masterpiece of the High Renaissance, which depicted the human body in perfect form after the model of antiquity.

title: Erasmus publishes the Greek New Testament
summary: The first printed edition of the New Testament in Greek, a key work of humanism, appears in Basel.
text: For his Novum Instrumentum, Erasmus of Rotterdam compared several manuscripts, set the original Greek text alongside a Latin translation of his own, and added critical notes. In doing so he called into question the Latin Vulgate, authoritative for centuries, and demanded that every Christian should read the Bible for himself. Luther used the second edition of 1519 for his German translation of the New Testament, and Tyndale and Calvin also built on it. Printing made the work available throughout Europe within a few years.

title: Luther publishes the 95 Theses
summary: The Wittenberg theologian Martin Luther criticizes the trade in indulgences in 95 theses and sets off the Reformation.
text: Luther opposed the idea that one could buy release from the punishment for sins by purchasing letters of indulgence. Thanks to printing, his theses spread across the whole of Germany within a few weeks. In 1521 he refused to recant at the Diet of Worms, was outlawed, and at the Wartburg translated the New Testament into German.

title: The first circumnavigation of the world under Magellan
summary: A Spanish fleet under Ferdinand Magellan sails around the earth for the first time and proves in practice that it is a sphere.
text: In the south of America Magellan found the strait named after him and crossed the Pacific, which he so named because of its calm sea. He himself died in 1521 in the Philippines in a fight with local people. Only one ship, the Victoria under Juan Sebastián Elcano, returned to Spain in 1522 with 18 survivors.

title: The fall of Tenochtitlan
summary: Spanish conquistadors under Hernán Cortés capture the capital of the Aztecs.
text: Cortés had landed in Mexico in 1519 with a few hundred soldiers and had allied himself with peoples who suffered under Aztec rule. After a siege lasting months, in which smallpox and hunger weakened the defenders, Tenochtitlan fell in August 1521. On the ruins of the city arose Mexico City, the capital of the Spanish viceroyalty of New Spain.

title: Diet of Worms: Luther refuses to recant
summary: Before Emperor Charles V, Martin Luther refuses to recant his teachings and is thereupon placed under the imperial ban.
text: After the pope had excommunicated Luther, the young emperor summoned him to Worms with a guarantee of safe conduct. On 18 April 1521 Luther declared before the emperor and the imperial estates that he could recant only if he were refuted from Holy Scripture, for to act against conscience was neither safe nor wholesome. The Edict of Worms declared him a heretic and banned his writings, but the elector Frederick the Wise had him abducted for appearance's sake and hidden at the Wartburg. There Luther translated the New Testament into German in just eleven weeks.

title: The German Peasants' War
summary: Peasants in southern and central Germany rise up against dues and serfdom and are bloodily put down.
text: Encouraged by the Reformation, the peasants demanded in the Twelve Articles of Memmingen the free election of pastors, the end of serfdom, and lower dues. Luther sharply condemned the revolt and took the side of the princes. The armies of the Swabian League defeated the peasants at Frankenhausen among other places; around 70,000 people lost their lives.

title: The beginning of the transatlantic slave trade
summary: For the first time, enslaved Africans are carried off directly from the West African coast to America.
text: Because the indigenous population of America was dying in great numbers from disease and violence, the colonial rulers looked for labor for plantations and mines. Portuguese and later Spanish, English, French, and Dutch traders bought or seized people on the African coast and carried them across the Atlantic under cruel conditions. By the 19th century more than twelve million people had been carried off in this way.

title: The conquest of the Inca empire
summary: Francisco Pizarro takes the Inca ruler Atahualpa prisoner and brings the largest empire in South America under Spanish control.
text: With fewer than 200 men, Pizarro lured the Inca Atahualpa into an ambush at Cajamarca and had his retinue slaughtered. Despite an enormous ransom in gold and silver, Atahualpa was executed in 1533. A preceding civil war and imported epidemics had weakened the empire; in 1535 the Spaniards founded Lima and exploited the silver mines of Potosí.

title: Copernicus publishes the heliocentric model of the universe
summary: In his principal work, Nicolaus Copernicus places the sun rather than the earth at the center of the universe.
text: The book De revolutionibus orbium coelestium appeared in Nuremberg shortly before the death of its author. Copernicus explained the movements of the planets more simply by having the earth circle the sun, and in doing so he contradicted the teaching of Ptolemy, which had been accepted since antiquity. His model was later confirmed and developed further by Kepler, Galileo, and Newton, and it marks the beginning of modern astronomy.

title: Vesalius founds modern anatomy
summary: With his work De humani corporis fabrica, Andreas Vesalius replaces the ancient teaching of Galen with observations of the dissected human body.
text: Vesalius, who came from Brussels, taught in Padua and dissected himself instead of watching an assistant and reading aloud from Galen, as was usual. In doing so he found more than 200 errors in ancient anatomy, which Galen had derived from animals. His work in seven books, printed in Basel in 1543, combined precise descriptions with masterly woodcuts from the workshop of Titian. The Fabrica made the human body an object of independent research and became the foundation of scientific medicine.

title: Council of Trent
summary: The Catholic Church responds to the Reformation with a clarification of its teaching and with internal reforms.
text: In three sessions over 18 years, the bishops affirmed the Catholic doctrine of the sacraments, of tradition, and of justification, and marked it off clearly from the Protestant positions. At the same time abuses such as the sale of offices were combated and seminaries were established for better training. The council shaped Catholicism into the 20th century and deepened the division of Christendom.

title: Peace of Augsburg
summary: The Diet of Augsburg recognizes the Lutheran confession in the empire and leaves the choice of denomination to the territorial rulers.
text: After the Schmalkaldic War and the revolt of the princes, Charles V had come to see that the Protestants could not be forced back into the old church, and he left the negotiations to his brother Ferdinand. The peace proclaimed on 25 September 1555 granted each imperial estate the right to determine the Catholic or the Lutheran confession for its own territory; subjects of another faith were allowed to emigrate. Later this principle was summed up in the formula that whoever rules the land determines its religion. Calvinists remained excluded, and unresolved disputes contributed to the outbreak of the Thirty Years' War in 1618.

title: Akbar becomes ruler of the Mughal empire
summary: The thirteen-year-old Akbar ascends the throne and builds the Mughal empire into the dominant power in India with a policy of religious tolerance.
text: The Mughal empire had been founded by Babur in 1526, but it was Akbar who secured it for good: after his victory at the second battle of Panipat in 1556, he subdued northern India, Gujarat, and Bengal over the following decades. He bound the Hindu Rajputs to himself through marriages and offices, abolished the special tax on non-Muslims in 1564, and had Muslims, Hindus, Jains, Parsis, and Jesuits debate with one another at his court. His administration, with a land survey for taxation and a ranking order of officials, and the buildings of Fatehpur Sikri, shaped India into the British period.

title: Oda Nobunaga wins at Okehazama and begins the unification of Japan
summary: With a surprise victory over a far superior army, the provincial lord Oda Nobunaga rises to become the leading power in a fragmented Japan.
text: Since the Ōnin War of 1467, Japan had been in the Sengoku period, the age of the warring states, broken up into dozens of principalities, while the shogun in Kyoto was powerless. In 1560 Nobunaga attacked the camp of the lord Imagawa Yoshimoto at Okehazama with a few thousand warriors and killed him. In the following years he took Kyoto, in 1575 at Nagashino deployed muskets in great numbers, which Portuguese traders had brought into the country, and broke the power of the Buddhist monasteries. After his death in 1582, Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Tokugawa Ieyasu completed the unification of the country.

title: St. Bartholomew's Day massacre in Paris
summary: In the night of 24 August 1572, thousands of Huguenots are murdered in Paris; the massacre becomes a symbol of the wars of religion.
text: Numerous Huguenot leaders had come to Paris for the wedding of the Protestant Henry of Navarre to Marguerite de Valois, the king's sister. After a failed attempt on the life of Admiral Coligny, the court, under the influence of the queen mother Catherine de' Medici, had the leaders killed; the mob widened the violence into a massacre that claimed up to 10,000 victims in Paris and the provinces. The pope had a commemorative medal struck; Protestant princes were appalled. The wars of religion ended only in 1598, when Henry IV, by then a Catholic, granted the Huguenots freedom of worship with the Edict of Nantes.

title: Introduction of the Gregorian calendar
summary: Pope Gregory XIII reforms the calendar: 4 October 1582 is followed immediately by 15 October.
text: The Julian calendar, in force since Caesar, had fallen ten days behind the solar year, so that Easter moved further and further away from the beginning of spring. A commission around the astronomer Christopher Clavius calculated a new rule for leap years, according to which full centuries are leap years only if they are divisible by 400. Catholic countries adopted the reform at once, the Protestant territories of Germany only in 1700, Great Britain in 1752, and Russia in 1918. Today the Gregorian calendar is the basis of the civil year worldwide.

title: The defeat of the Spanish Armada
summary: Philip II's invasion fleet fails in the English Channel against the English fleet and against storms; England holds its own as a Protestant sea power.
text: With around 130 ships Philip II intended to ferry an army from the Netherlands to England in order to overthrow Elizabeth I and restore Catholicism. The more maneuverable English ships under Howard and Drake fired on the Armada from a distance, fireships broke up its formation off Calais, and at Gravelines it suffered heavy losses. On the way home around Scotland and Ireland, storms destroyed a large part of the fleet; only about two thirds of the ships returned. The victory consolidated Elizabeth's rule, strengthened English self-confidence, and set in motion England's rise as a sea power.

title: The Thirty Years' War
summary: A war of religion and power devastates the Holy Roman Empire and draws in almost all the European powers.
text: The war began with the Defenestration of Prague, when Protestant Bohemian nobles threw imperial governors out of a window. After victories by the emperor, Denmark, Sweden under Gustavus Adolphus, and finally Catholic France intervened on the Protestant side. Mercenary armies, hunger, and epidemics killed more than a third of the population in some regions of Germany.

title: The height of the witch hunts
summary: In the years around 1630 the witch trials in central Europe reach their peak, with thousands of executions.
text: Between about 1560 and 1630, tens of thousands of people in Europe were accused as witches, forced under torture to confess, and burned; most of the victims were women, and many trials took place in the prince-bishoprics of Würzburg, Bamberg, and Cologne. The hardship of war, crop failures, and the expectation that the devil worked harm with the help of witches fueled the persecution. In 1631 the Jesuit Friedrich Spee criticized torture in the Cautio Criminalis as a source of false confessions. The trials ended only in the 18th century; the last execution in Europe took place in Switzerland in 1782.

title: The trial of Galileo Galilei
summary: The Roman Inquisition condemns Galileo for his defense of the heliocentric model and forces him to recant.
text: In his Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems of 1632, Galileo had presented the teaching of Copernicus so convincingly that the church saw in it a violation of the prohibition of 1616. On 22 June 1633, almost seventy years old, he had to abjure on his knees in Rome and was sentenced to lifelong house arrest. In his villa near Florence he nevertheless wrote the Discorsi on mechanics and the laws of falling bodies, which appeared in the Netherlands in 1638. The trial became a symbol of the conflict between science and the authority of faith; the church rehabilitated Galileo only in 1992.

title: The closing of Japan under the Tokugawa
summary: The Tokugawa shogunate bars the Portuguese from entering, forbids Japanese to leave the country, and allows only the Dutch and the Chinese limited trade at Nagasaki.
text: Tokugawa Ieyasu had founded the shogunate in 1603 and pacified Japan after a century of civil war. His successors feared that Christian missionaries and European traders might undermine the established order, especially since a revolt of Christian peasants at Shimabara had to be bloodily put down in 1637. Through a series of decrees between 1633 and 1639, Christianity was banned, the building of ocean-going ships was forbidden, and foreign trade was restricted to the artificial island of Dejima off Nagasaki. This policy, known as sakoku, lasted until 1854 and gave Japan more than two centuries of peace and a culture of its own.

title: The English Civil War and the execution of Charles I
summary: In the struggle between king and parliament the parliamentary army wins; in 1649 Charles I becomes the first European monarch to be executed in public.
text: Charles I had ruled for eleven years without parliament and had tried to force an episcopal church on Scotland, until lack of money compelled him to summon parliament in 1640. The dispute over taxes, religion, and command of the army escalated into civil war in 1642 between royalists and parliamentary troops, in which Oliver Cromwell's New Model Army forced the decision at Naseby in 1645. A parliament purged by the army condemned the king for high treason, and on 30 January 1649 he was beheaded in front of his palace in London. England became a republic, and from 1653 a protectorate under Cromwell; in 1660 the monarchy returned under Charles II.

title: Peace of Westphalia
summary: In Münster and Osnabrück the first great European peace congress brings the Thirty Years' War to an end.
text: After five years of negotiations, Catholics, Lutherans, and Calvinists in the empire received equal rights, and the territorial rulers gained far-reaching sovereignty. France and Sweden received territories, and the independence of the Netherlands and of Switzerland was recognized. The peace is regarded as the birth of the modern system of states, in which sovereign states regulate their relations by treaty.

title: Founding of the Royal Society
summary: In London, scholars found a society for the advancement of scientific knowledge through experiment and exchange.
text: After a lecture by the architect Christopher Wren, twelve men, among them Robert Boyle, resolved on 28 November 1660 to form a society for the advancement of knowledge about nature; in 1662 it received a royal charter. Its motto Nullius in verba, on no one's word, expressed the principle that only experiment and observation should count as proof. From 1665 the Philosophical Transactions appeared, the oldest scientific journal still in existence, and Robert Hooke as curator demonstrated experiments every week. Newton headed the society from 1703 until his death; academies in Paris, Berlin, and St Petersburg were founded on its model.

title: Louis XIV moves the court to Versailles
summary: The Sun King makes the magnificent palace of Versailles the permanent seat of government and court.
text: Out of a hunting lodge belonging to his father, Louis XIV had an enormous complex built over decades, with the Hall of Mirrors and its gardens. The nobility was tied to the court, where it competed for the king's favor in a strictly regulated ceremonial and was thereby deprived of political power. Versailles became the model for palaces throughout Europe and a symbol of absolutism.

title: The second siege of Vienna by the Ottomans
summary: A relief army under the Polish king John III Sobieski defeats the Ottoman army before Vienna and begins the Ottoman withdrawal from central Europe.
text: In July 1683 the grand vizier Kara Mustafa encircled Vienna with around 150,000 men, and the garrison and citizens held the city for two months while Emperor Leopold I had fled. On 12 September an army of imperial, Polish, Bavarian, and Saxon troops attacked down from the Kahlenberg; the charge of the Polish cavalry decided the battle. In the Great Turkish War that followed, the Habsburgs conquered Hungary and Transylvania, which the Treaty of Karlowitz confirmed in 1699. Austria thus became a great power in southeastern Europe, and Ottoman expansion in Europe was at an end.

title: Edict of Fontainebleau: the expulsion of the Huguenots
summary: Louis XIV revokes the Edict of Nantes and forbids Protestant worship in France; hundreds of thousands of Huguenots flee.
text: For the Sun King, the unity of the state included the unity of faith, and even before 1685 billeted dragoons had forced Protestant families to convert. The edict of October 1685 had the churches of the Huguenots torn down, banished their pastors, and at the same time forbade the faithful to emigrate. Nevertheless some 200,000 people fled, many of them craftsmen, merchants, and officers, to the Netherlands, England, Switzerland, and Brandenburg, which invited them with the Edict of Potsdam. France lost valuable skilled workers, and the thinkers of the Enlightenment saw in the edict an example of the consequences of religious intolerance.

title: Newton publishes the Principia
summary: With the laws of motion and the law of gravitation, Isaac Newton founds classical physics.
text: In the Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica, Newton showed that the same force makes an apple fall to the ground and holds the moon in its orbit. The movements of the planets, the tides, and the trajectory of projectiles could now be calculated with a few mathematical laws. The work became the model for a science that understands nature as governed by law and open to calculation.

title: The Glorious Revolution in England
summary: The English parliament drives out the Catholic king James II and establishes the supremacy of parliament.
text: Parliament called the Protestant William of Orange and his wife Mary into the country, whereupon James II fled to France almost without a fight. In 1689 the new rulers had to accept the Bill of Rights, which secured for parliament the right to grant taxes, free elections, and freedom of speech. England thus became a constitutional monarchy and a counter-model to absolutism.

title: Locke publishes the Two Treatises of Government
summary: John Locke bases rule on the consent of the governed and on the protection of life, liberty, and property.
text: Shortly after the Glorious Revolution, Locke's Two Treatises of Government appeared anonymously, in which he refuted the doctrine of the divine right of kings. Human beings, he argued, are by nature free and equal and join together in a state only in order to secure their natural rights; a government that violates these rights may be removed. In the same year his Letter Concerning Toleration appeared, and his Essay Concerning Human Understanding, which traced all knowledge back to experience. Locke's ideas shaped the American Declaration of Independence and liberal political theory to this day.

title: Peter the Great founds St Petersburg
summary: In the marshland on the Neva, the tsar has a new capital built as a window on Europe.
text: During the Great Northern War against Sweden, Peter I laid out the Peter and Paul Fortress on conquered land by the Baltic, and from it the city grew. Tens of thousands of forced laborers died during the building work on the marshy ground. In 1712 St Petersburg became the capital of Russia and remained so until 1918; the city symbolized the opening of the empire to the west.

title: The Qianlong Emperor and the height of the Qing dynasty
summary: Under the Qianlong Emperor, China reaches its greatest extent and a golden age of culture.
text: Qianlong reigned from 1735 to 1796 and extended the empire through campaigns into Central Asia, Tibet, and the southwest. The population grew to around 300 million, and the emperor had an enormous collection of Chinese literature compiled. Toward European wishes for trade, China remained closed; in 1793 Qianlong turned away a British embassy with the remark that his empire had no need of foreign goods.

title: Maria Theresa and the War of the Austrian Succession
summary: After the death of Emperor Charles VI, Prussia, Bavaria, and France attack the inheritance of the 23-year-old Maria Theresa, who holds on to her lands except for Silesia.
text: Charles VI had secured his daughter's succession with the Pragmatic Sanction, but he had hardly died in October 1740 when Frederick II of Prussia invaded the wealthy province of Silesia, and Bavaria and France put forward claims of their own. Maria Theresa won the support of the Hungarian estates, raised new armies, and in 1745 secured the election of her husband Francis Stephen as emperor. The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle in 1748 confirmed her possessions but left Silesia with Prussia. From the defeat she drew the conclusion that the administration, army, taxes, and school system of her lands had to be fundamentally reformed.

title: Montesquieu publishes The Spirit of the Laws
summary: Charles de Montesquieu calls for the separation of legislative, executive, and judicial power in order to secure liberty against the abuse of power.
text: The baron from Bordeaux had spent twenty years comparing the constitutions, climates, customs, and laws of different peoples, and had traveled in England. In his work, printed in Geneva, he described the English constitution as a model, because there the king, parliament, and independent courts limited one another; where all power lies in one hand, he wrote, there is no liberty. He distinguished between republic, monarchy, and despotism and warned against arbitrary rule. Although the church placed the book on the Index in 1751, it was read throughout Europe and influenced the Constitution of the United States of 1787 as well as the French revolutionaries.

title: The first volumes of the Encyclopédie appear
summary: Denis Diderot and Jean le Rond d'Alembert publish the first volume of the great encyclopedia of the Enlightenment in Paris.
text: The Encyclopédie was to gather the entire knowledge of the age, from philosophy to the crafts, and make it accessible to reason. More than 140 authors, among them Voltaire, Rousseau, and Montesquieu, wrote articles that often criticized the church and absolutism in veiled form. Despite bans and censorship, the work grew by 1772 to 28 volumes with more than 70,000 articles and was read throughout Europe.

title: The Lisbon earthquake
summary: On All Saints' Day, an earthquake, a tidal wave, and fires destroy the Portuguese capital and set off a debate across Europe about God and nature.
text: On the morning of 1 November 1755, when the churches were full, a tremendous earthquake shook Lisbon; tidal waves flooded the harbor, and fires raged for days. Estimates range from 30,000 to 60,000 dead, and one of the richest cities in Europe lay in ruins. The minister Pombal organized rescue and reconstruction with earthquake-resistant buildings and had the causes investigated scientifically. In a poem and in Candide, Voltaire mocked the idea that everything in the world is ordered for the best, Rousseau contradicted him, and Kant wrote three treatises on the natural causes of earthquakes.

title: The Seven Years' War
summary: Prussia and Great Britain fight against Austria, France, and Russia in a war waged in Europe, America, and India.
text: Frederick II of Prussia opened the war with the invasion of Saxony and held his own against superior forces, but he came close to defeat several times; the death of the Russian tsarina Elizabeth in 1762 saved him. In North America and India, Great Britain defeated France and took over Canada as well as supremacy in Bengal. Prussia kept Silesia and rose to become a European great power.

title: James Cook's Pacific voyages
summary: On three voyages James Cook surveys New Zealand, the east coast of Australia, and countless islands of the Pacific, and ends the search for the southern continent.
text: On the commission of the Royal Society, Cook observed the transit of Venus on Tahiti in 1769, then sailed around New Zealand and in 1770 landed in Botany Bay on the east coast of Australia, which he claimed for Great Britain. On the second voyage he was the first to cross the Antarctic Circle and proved that there was no habitable southern continent; on the third he reached Hawaii, where he was killed in a dispute with local people in 1779. With a chronometer, sauerkraut against scurvy, and naturalists such as Joseph Banks and Georg Forster on board, his voyages turned exploration into a science. For the inhabitants of Australia and the Pacific islands, European colonization began with them.

title: James Watt improves the steam engine
summary: The Scottish instrument maker James Watt receives a patent for a steam engine with a separate condenser.
text: Thomas Newcomen's steam engine had been used since 1712 to pump water out of mines, but it consumed enormous quantities of coal. Watt recognized that the steam should be condensed in a separate vessel so that the cylinder stays hot; this reduced fuel consumption by about three quarters. Together with the entrepreneur Matthew Boulton he built engines from 1775 onward that soon drove factories, mills, and mines.

title: The American Declaration of Independence
summary: On 4 July 1776, thirteen British colonies declare themselves the independent United States of America.
text: The dispute with London over taxes and representation had turned into open fighting in 1775. The text, written by Thomas Jefferson, justified the separation by the inalienable rights of all people to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. After the victory at Yorktown in 1781, Great Britain recognized independence in 1783; in 1787 the states gave themselves a federal constitution.

title: The power loom and the factory system
summary: Spinning machines and the power loom move textile production out of the home and into the factory.
text: With James Hargreaves's spinning jenny of the 1760s, one worker could operate several spindles at once, Richard Arkwright's water frame used water power from 1769, and in 1785 Edmund Cartwright patented the power loom. Because the machines were tied to a central source of power, large factories arose such as Arkwright's mill at Cromford, in which hundreds of people worked to fixed hours and under supervision. The handloom weavers could not compete with the cheap factory cloth and fell into poverty. The factory system spread from the cotton industry to all branches of industry and has shaped the world of work to this day.

title: The Constitution of the United States
summary: In Philadelphia the delegates of the states adopt the first modern written constitution, with a separation of powers and an elected president.
text: After the War of Independence the thirteen states formed only a loose confederation without powers of taxation or trade, which led to debt, unrest, and quarrels. From May to September 1787, 55 delegates under the chairmanship of George Washington deliberated on a new order in Philadelphia behind closed doors; James Madison is regarded as its most important architect. The constitution divided power between a Congress of two chambers, a president, and a Supreme Court, and between the federal government and the individual states; a compromise counted enslaved people as three fifths for the allocation of seats and thereby entrenched slavery. After fierce debates it came into force in 1789, and in 1791 ten amendments, the Bill of Rights, added basic rights such as freedom of speech, of the press, and of religion. The constitution remains in force, with amendments, to this day.

title: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen
summary: On 26 August 1789 the National Assembly proclaims liberty, equality, and the sovereignty of the people as basic rights.
text: In 17 articles the assembly declared that all human beings are born free and equal in rights, that all state power proceeds from the people, and that freedom of opinion and of religion, property, and protection against arbitrary treatment are to be guaranteed. Women, slaves, and those without property remained excluded at first; in 1791 Olympe de Gouges responded with a Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen. The declaration became a model for constitutions all over the world.

title: The Women's March on Versailles
summary: Thousands of Parisian women march to Versailles because of the shortage of bread and force the royal family to move to Paris.
text: In the autumn of 1789 the price of bread rose in Paris, while the king had still not confirmed the resolutions of the National Assembly, and rumors of a banquet held by the guard at Versailles increased the anger. On 5 October some 7,000 women of the market halls, armed with pikes and kitchen knives, marched the twenty kilometers to Versailles in the rain; the National Guard under Lafayette followed them. After the palace was stormed during the night, in which members of the bodyguard were killed, Louis XVI had to sign the Declaration of the Rights of Man and move with his family to the Tuileries in Paris, where the National Assembly followed as well. From then on the king stood before the eyes of the people, and women had shown themselves to be a political force of the revolution.

title: The storming of the Bastille
summary: On 14 July 1789 the people of Paris storm the royal prison, marking the beginning of the French Revolution.
text: After the Third Estate had declared itself the National Assembly and the king had gathered troops around Paris, the population armed itself. The Bastille held only a few prisoners but was regarded as a symbol of royal arbitrariness. Its fall forced Louis XVI to give way; throughout the country peasants rose against their landlords, and in August the National Assembly abolished feudal rights.

title: The beginning of the Haitian Revolution
summary: In the French colony of Saint-Domingue, the enslaved rise up against their masters.
text: Through its sugar and coffee plantations, Saint-Domingue was the richest colony of France, in which half a million slaves worked under cruel conditions. The uprising of August 1791 grew under the leadership of Toussaint Louverture into a war lasting years, in which the insurgents held their own against the French, the Spanish, and the British. In 1794 France abolished slavery; after Napoleon's attempt to reintroduce it, Haiti declared its independence in 1804.

title: The execution of Louis XVI and the Reign of Terror
summary: The king is guillotined, and the Committee of Public Safety under Robespierre establishes the rule of terror.
text: After his failed attempt to flee and the fall of the monarchy, Louis XVI was condemned for treason and executed on 21 January 1793. War against almost all of Europe, uprisings in the Vendée, and shortages of supplies led to the dictatorship of the Committee of Public Safety; by the summer of 1794 revolutionary tribunals had around 17,000 people executed, among them Queen Marie-Antoinette and Olympe de Gouges. In July 1794 Robespierre himself was overthrown and guillotined.

title: France abolishes slavery
summary: On 4 February 1794 the National Convention abolishes slavery in all French colonies, under the pressure of the uprising in Saint-Domingue.
text: Despite the Declaration of the Rights of Man, the National Assembly had at first left slavery in the colonies untouched, because planters and port cities profited from the sugar trade. Only the uprising in Saint-Domingue and the war against Spain and Great Britain forced the commissioners of the republic in 1793 to declare the enslaved free, in order to win them as soldiers. When a delegation from the colony, including the former slave Jean-Baptiste Belley, appeared before the Convention in February 1794, it resolved without a dissenting vote to abolish slavery in all colonies and to grant citizenship to all men regardless of the color of their skin. Napoleon reintroduced slavery in 1802, which rekindled the struggle for freedom in Haiti; France abolished it for good only in 1848.

title: Napoleon's Egyptian campaign
summary: Napoleon occupies Egypt in order to strike at Great Britain's route to India; the campaign fails, but it founds the modern study of ancient Egypt.
text: In July 1798 Napoleon landed in Egypt with 35,000 soldiers; the country formally belonged to the Ottoman Empire but was ruled by the Mamluks, and he defeated their cavalry at the Battle of the Pyramids. A few days later the British fleet under Nelson destroyed the French ships at Aboukir, so that the army was cut off from supplies; an advance into Syria failed before Acre in 1799. Napoleon left his army secretly in order to seize power in Paris; the remnants surrendered to the British in 1801. The 167 scholars who had accompanied him surveyed temples, pyramids, and wildlife and published their results in the Description de l'Égypte; the Rosetta Stone, found in 1799, enabled Champollion to decipher the hieroglyphs in 1822. In Egypt itself the campaign set in motion the rise of Muhammad Ali and the modernization of the country.

title: The Code civil comes into force
summary: Napoleon gives France a uniform civil code that establishes equality before the law and freedom of property.
text: The Code civil replaced hundreds of regional legal systems with a single code of more than 2,000 articles. It guaranteed the equality of all men before the law, freedom of contract and of trade, private property, and civil marriage, but it placed women under the guardianship of father or husband. It was introduced in the territories ruled by France, such as the Rhineland, the Netherlands, and Italy, and in part remained in force into the 20th century.

title: Napoleon crowns himself emperor
summary: In the cathedral of Notre-Dame, Napoleon Bonaparte places the imperial crown on his own head on 2 December 1804.
text: After the coup of 1799, Napoleon had stabilized France as First Consul and had himself confirmed by plebiscite. Pope Pius VII was present at the coronation, but Napoleon crowned himself and then his wife Joséphine, in order to show that he owed his power to no one. As Emperor of the French he led Europe into a decade of wars and reshaped the continent according to his will.

title: The independence of Haiti
summary: On 1 January 1804 Jean-Jacques Dessalines declares the independence of Haiti, the first state founded by formerly enslaved people.
text: After Napoleon had sent an army to Saint-Domingue in 1802 to restore slavery, and after Toussaint Louverture had been carried off into captivity, Jean-Jacques Dessalines and Alexandre Pétion carried on the resistance. Yellow fever and the guerrilla warfare of the former slaves wore down the French troops; after the defeat at Vertières in November 1803 the French evacuated the colony. On 1 January 1804 Dessalines proclaimed independence at Gonaïves and gave the country its old indigenous name, Haiti; massacres of the remaining French followed. Haiti became the second independent republic of the Americas, but it remained isolated by the slaveholding powers; France recognized it only in 1825, in return for an indemnity of 150 million francs that burdened the country for more than a century.

title: The end of the Holy Roman Empire
summary: On 6 August 1806 Emperor Francis II lays down the imperial crown; the empire, more than 800 years old, ceases to exist.
text: After Austria's defeat at Austerlitz in 1805, Napoleon reordered Germany as he saw fit: Bavaria and Württemberg became kingdoms, and in July 1806 16 southern and western German states joined together under his protection in the Confederation of the Rhine and left the empire. As early as 1803, the Final Recess of the Imperial Deputation had dissolved the ecclesiastical principalities and most of the imperial cities and distributed their territories among larger states. In response to Napoleon's ultimatum, Francis II, who in 1804 had prudently raised himself to Emperor of Austria, declared the empire extinguished on 6 August 1806 and released all the estates from their obligations. The end of the empire, which had existed since Otto the Great, provoked hardly any resistance; Goethe noted that a quarrel involving his coachman had excited him more. The German question, how the many states should be joined together in future, remained open until 1871.

title: The Prussian reforms
summary: After the defeat by Napoleon, Stein, Hardenberg, Scharnhorst, and Humboldt modernize the Prussian state from above.
text: In 1806 Napoleon had crushingly defeated the Prussian army at Jena and Auerstedt; the Peace of Tilsit in 1807 took half its territory from Prussia and forced it to make heavy payments. To save the state, the minister Baron vom Stein and, after him, Hardenberg began reforms intended to turn subjects into citizens: the October Edict of 1807 abolished the hereditary subjection of the peasants, the Municipal Ordinance of 1808 gave the towns self-government, in 1810 freedom of trade followed, and in 1812 the edict on the civil equality of the Jews. Scharnhorst and Gneisenau created an army of citizens that promoted officers by ability rather than by noble birth and received universal conscription in 1814; Wilhelm von Humboldt reformed the schools and founded the University of Berlin in 1810. The reforms remained unfinished, and a constitution was promised but not granted, yet they laid the foundation for Prussia's rise in the 19th century.

title: Napoleon's Russian campaign
summary: The Grande Armée marches on Moscow with more than 600,000 men and is almost completely destroyed on the retreat by cold, hunger, and fighting.
text: Because Tsar Alexander I no longer observed the Continental System against Great Britain, Napoleon crossed the Russian border on 24 June 1812 with the largest army Europe had ever seen; only a third of the soldiers were French, the rest Germans, Poles, Italians, and other allies. The Russians fell back and burned the land behind them, gave battle at Borodino on 7 September in the bloodiest engagement of the campaign, and abandoned Moscow, which went up in flames shortly after the French entered. Since the tsar would not negotiate, Napoleon ordered the retreat on 19 October, and with winter setting in early, with hunger and constant attacks by Cossacks, it became a catastrophe; at the crossing of the Berezina at the end of November the army finally fell apart. Barely more than 50,000 men returned. The defeat encouraged Prussia and Austria to ally with Russia and set off the Wars of Liberation.

title: The Battle of the Nations at Leipzig
summary: The armies of Russia, Prussia, Austria, and Sweden defeat Napoleon in the largest battle before the 20th century.
text: After the destruction of the Grande Armée in Russia in 1812, Prussia and then Austria rose against French rule. From 16 to 19 October 1813 some 600,000 soldiers fought at Leipzig; more than 90,000 were killed or wounded. Napoleon had to withdraw across the Rhine, lost control of Germany, and abdicated in April 1814 after the allies marched into Paris.

title: The Congress of Vienna
summary: Under the direction of the Austrian foreign minister Metternich, the European powers reorder Europe after the fall of Napoleon.
text: Representatives of almost all the European states negotiated in Vienna over borders and forms of rule; the guiding ideas were the restoration of the old dynasties, a balance among the great powers, and solidarity against revolutions. In place of the Holy Roman Empire, dissolved in 1806, came the German Confederation of 39 states. The settlement protected Europe from major wars for decades, but it suppressed liberal and national movements with censorship and police.

title: The Battle of Waterloo
summary: Wellington and Blücher defeat Napoleon for good on 18 June 1815; he is banished to St Helena.
