text: In March 1815 Napoleon returned from the island of Elba to France, where the troops went over to him and Louis XVIII fled; the powers assembled in Vienna declared him an enemy of mankind. Napoleon attacked the armies standing in Belgium before they could unite, and on 16 June he defeated the Prussians at Ligny. On 18 June, at Waterloo south of Brussels, Wellington's British, Dutch, and German army withstood the French attacks all day, until in the evening Blücher's Prussians arrived and decided the issue; around 50,000 soldiers were killed or wounded. Napoleon abdicated for the second time and was taken by the British to the Atlantic island of St Helena, where he died in 1821. The rule of the Hundred Days was over, and the Second Peace of Paris imposed on France the loss of territory, occupation, and reparations.

title: Bolívar and the independence of South America
summary: Simón Bolívar defeats the Spanish at Boyacá and founds the republic of Gran Colombia.
text: From 1810 the Spanish colonies of America fought for their independence, encouraged by the example of the United States and by the weakness of Spain under Napoleonic occupation. In 1819 Bolívar crossed the Andes with his army and defeated the Spanish at Boyacá, whereupon Gran Colombia arose out of the present-day states of Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, and Panama. In the south José de San Martín liberated Argentina and Chile; in 1824, with the battle of Ayacucho, the last Spanish stronghold in Peru fell.

title: The independence of Mexico
summary: Eleven years after the call to arms by the priest Hidalgo, New Spain separates from Spain and becomes independent as Mexico.
text: On 16 September 1810 the parish priest Miguel Hidalgo called on the population in the village of Dolores to rise against Spanish colonial rule; tens of thousands of indigenous people and mestizos followed him, but they were defeated in 1811, and Hidalgo was executed. His successor José María Morelos carried on the struggle, called a congress, and in 1815 likewise died before a firing squad. When a liberal revolution broke out in Spain in 1820, the royal officer Agustín de Iturbide changed sides and agreed with the rebel leader Vicente Guerrero on the Plan of Iguala, which promised independence, Catholicism, and equality for all inhabitants. On 27 September 1821 the army entered Mexico City; Iturbide had himself crowned emperor but was overthrown in 1823, and in 1824 Mexico gave itself a republican constitution. 16 September is still the national holiday today.

title: The first public railway, Stockton–Darlington
summary: The first public railway with a steam locomotive runs in northern England.
text: On 27 September 1825 the locomotive Locomotion No. 1, built by George Stephenson, pulled a train carrying coal and passengers over the roughly 40 kilometers between Stockton and Darlington. The line was the first public railway to use steam locomotives permanently. Within a few decades a network of rails covered Europe and North America and made the transport of goods and people faster and cheaper than ever before.

title: The July Revolution in Paris
summary: In three days of fighting at the barricades, Paris overthrows the Bourbon king Charles X; Louis-Philippe becomes the Citizen King, and the revolution has effects in Belgium, Poland, and Germany.
text: King Charles X tried to extend the power of the crown against parliament and on 25 July 1830 issued ordinances that abolished freedom of the press, restricted the franchise, and dissolved the chamber that had just been elected. Journalists, students, craftsmen, and workers thereupon put up barricades, and in the three glorious days from 27 to 29 July they captured the city hall and the Louvre; around 800 insurgents died. Charles X fled to England, and the liberal citizenry, with Lafayette's support, installed the Duke of Orléans as Louis-Philippe I, King of the French, who adopted the tricolor and swore an oath to the constitution. The revolution set off the revolt of Belgium against the Netherlands, the Polish November Uprising against Russia, and unrest in several German states; Delacroix's painting Liberty Leading the People became its emblem.

title: The Hambach Festival
summary: Around 30,000 people gather at Hambach Castle to demand freedom, German unity, and understanding among nations; it is the largest political rally of the Vormärz.
text: After the July Revolution, resentment over censorship, taxes, and arbitrary policing had also built up in the Bavarian Palatinate; the Carlsbad Decrees of 1819 had placed the press and the universities throughout Germany under supervision. The journalists Philipp Jakob Siebenpfeiffer and Johann Georg August Wirth issued an invitation to a popular festival, and from 27 to 30 May 1832 craftsmen, peasants, students, and townspeople, among them many women as well as Polish and French guests, marched under black-red-gold flags to Hambach Castle near Neustadt an der Weinstraße. The speakers demanded freedom of the press, a constitution, national unity, and a Europe of free peoples; an uprising, however, was not resolved upon. The German Confederation responded with a ban on political associations and assemblies and had the organizers put on trial. The festival is regarded as the cradle of German democracy, and black-red-gold became the national colors in 1848 and 1919.

title: The abolition of slavery in the British Empire
summary: The British parliament resolves to free around 800,000 enslaved people in the colonies.
text: After Great Britain had already banned the slave trade in 1807, abolitionists such as William Wilberforce, mass petitions, and slave revolts in the Caribbean brought about the abolition of slavery itself. The Slavery Abolition Act of 1833 came into force on 1 August 1834; the slaveholders received 20 million pounds in compensation, while those set free had at first to go on working for years as so-called apprentices. France followed in 1848, the United States in 1865, Brazil only in 1888. From then on the British fleet hunted slave ships in the Atlantic, which at the same time served as a justification for the extension of British power in Africa.

title: The First Opium War
summary: Great Britain forces China open to trade with gunboats.
text: British merchants sold large quantities of opium from India to China and thereby balanced their trade. When the Chinese government stopped the smuggling in 1839 and had opium destroyed, Great Britain sent a fleet. In the Treaty of Nanking of 1842, China had to cede Hong Kong, open five ports, and pay heavy indemnities. The war began what is known as China's century of humiliation.

title: The weavers' uprising in Silesia
summary: Impoverished handloom weavers rise against the manufacturers and are put down by the Prussian military.
text: The cotton weavers in the Owl Mountains of Silesia could no longer keep up with English machine-made cloth and received ever lower wages from the merchant clothiers. On 4 June 1844 hundreds of weavers in Peterswaldau and Langenbielau marched to the houses of the manufacturers and destroyed machines and account books. Prussian soldiers fired into the crowd, eleven people died, and the leaders were sentenced to the penitentiary. The uprising made the social question a subject of debate throughout Germany; Heinrich Heine wrote the poem The Silesian Weavers, and Gerhart Hauptmann the drama The Weavers in 1892.

title: The Great Famine in Ireland
summary: Potato blight destroys the harvests; around a million Irish starve to death, and further millions emigrate.
text: The poor rural population of Ireland lived almost entirely on potatoes. When from 1845 onward a fungus destroyed the harvests for several years in succession, hundreds of thousands starved or died of typhus and cholera, while grain and cattle continued to be exported to England. The British government trusted in the free market and helped too late and too little. The population of Ireland fell from around 8.5 million to 6.5 million in the year 1851; millions of Irish emigrated to North America, and the memory of the famine fueled Irish nationalism.

title: The Communist Manifesto
summary: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels publish the programmatic text of the communist movement.
text: In February 1848, shortly before the outbreak of the European revolutions, the Manifesto of the Communist Party appeared in London. In it Marx and Engels described history as a succession of class struggles and predicted that the proletariat would overthrow the bourgeoisie. The text ends with the call, workers of all countries, unite. It became one of the most influential political texts in history.

title: The March Revolution of 1848 and the Frankfurt National Assembly
summary: A wave of revolution sweeps across Europe; the first all-German parliament assembles in the Paulskirche in Frankfurt.
text: After the February Revolution in Paris, people in Vienna, Berlin, and many German states demanded freedom of the press, constitutions, and national unity in March 1848; Metternich fled, and in Berlin hundreds of citizens died in fighting at the barricades. The National Assembly elected to the Paulskirche adopted basic rights and a constitution for a German empire. When the Prussian king Frederick William IV refused the imperial crown in 1849, the revolution failed, and the princes restored the old order.

title: The Sepoy Mutiny in India
summary: Indian soldiers mutiny against the British East India Company; afterward the Crown takes over the rule of India.
text: The trigger in May 1857 was the rumor that the cartridges of new rifles were greased with beef and pork fat, which offended Hindus and Muslims alike among the native soldiers, the sepoys. The mutiny at Meerut grew into an uprising across northern India; the rebels took Delhi and proclaimed the old Mughal emperor as their ruler. British troops put down the revolt by 1858 with extreme severity. The East India Company was dissolved, India was placed directly under the British Crown, and in 1876 Queen Victoria assumed the title Empress of India.

title: Darwin publishes On the Origin of Species
summary: Charles Darwin explains the diversity of life through evolution and natural selection.
text: On 24 November 1859 Darwin's book On the Origin of Species appeared in London, and its first edition sold out the same day. Drawing on observations from his voyage around the world on the Beagle and on decades of research, Darwin showed that species are not unchangeable but develop from common ancestors through natural selection. The theory contradicted the literal reading of the biblical account of creation and set off fierce debates. It became the foundation of modern biology, but it was also misused to justify racism and imperialism through what is known as Social Darwinism.

title: The American Civil War
summary: The Northern and Southern states of the USA fight over the unity of the Union and the abolition of slavery.
text: After the election of Abraham Lincoln, eleven Southern states left the Union because they saw slavery under threat. The war claimed more than 600,000 lives and was the first in which the railroad, the telegraph and industrial weapons production played a decisive role. Slavery was abolished by the Emancipation Proclamation of 1863 and the Thirteenth Amendment of 1865; the surrender of the Southern states preserved the unity of the United States.

title: Founding of the Red Cross
summary: An organization to care for wounded soldiers is created in Geneva on the initiative of Henry Dunant.
text: In 1859 Henry Dunant had witnessed the suffering of the wounded after the Battle of Solferino, and in his book A Memory of Solferino he called for voluntary relief societies and an international agreement to protect the wounded. In February 1863 he founded, together with four other citizens of Geneva, the committee from which the International Committee of the Red Cross emerged; in October the first international conference met. On 22 August 1864 twelve states signed the first Geneva Convention, which placed medical personnel, field hospitals and the wounded under the protection of the red cross on a white ground. This marked the beginning of modern international humanitarian law.

title: Meiji Restoration in Japan
summary: Japan ends the rule of the shoguns and modernizes along Western lines.
text: After American warships had forced Japan to open up in 1853, reform-minded samurai overthrew the shogunate in 1868 and placed the young Emperor Meiji at the head of the state. The new government abolished the system of social estates, introduced compulsory schooling and military service, and had railways, factories and a modern fleet built. Within a single generation Japan became the first industrial power in Asia and in 1905 even defeated Russia.

title: Opening of the Suez Canal
summary: The canal between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea shortens the sea route to Asia by thousands of kilometers.
text: Under the direction of the Frenchman Ferdinand de Lesseps, tens of thousands of Egyptian laborers dug a canal 160 kilometers long through the Isthmus of Suez over ten years. Ships sailing from Europe to India no longer had to travel around Africa. In 1875 Britain bought the Egyptian shares in the canal and occupied the country in 1882 in order to secure the lifeline of its colonial empire.

title: Founding of the German Empire
summary: After the victory over France, William I is proclaimed German Emperor at Versailles.
text: In three wars against Denmark, Austria and France, Otto von Bismarck had united the German states under Prussian leadership. On 18 January 1871 the Prussian king William I was proclaimed German Emperor in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles. The new empire was a constitutional monarchy with universal male suffrage for the Reichstag, but with a strong position for the emperor and the chancellor. It quickly became the leading industrial power on the continent.

title: Bismarck's Social Legislation
summary: The German Empire becomes the first state in the world to introduce health, accident and pension insurance.
text: Bismarck pursued a twofold strategy: with the Anti-Socialist Law of 1878 he banned the Social Democrats, while with the social legislation he sought to show workers that the state was looking after them. Health insurance came in 1883, accident insurance in 1884 and old-age and invalidity insurance in 1889, which paid a small pension from the age of 70. Employers and employees paid contributions, and the state added subsidies. The Social Democrats were not won over and became the strongest party in 1890, but the model of social insurance found imitators throughout the world and remains the foundation of the German welfare state to this day.

title: Berlin Conference Partitions Africa
summary: The European powers agree in Berlin on rules for dividing Africa into colonies.
text: At Bismarck's invitation, representatives of 13 European states and the United States met in order to avoid conflict over the Congo and the African coasts. Not a single African took part. The conference laid down that territorial claims had to be backed by actual occupation, and thereby set off the scramble for Africa. By around 1914 every territory on the continent apart from Ethiopia and Liberia was under European rule.

title: Congo Free State under Leopold II
summary: The Belgian king receives the Congo as personal property and exploits it through a brutal system of forced labor.
text: At the Berlin Conference in 1885 the powers recognized the Congo Free State as the personal property of Leopold II, who promised to promote trade and civilization. In reality his colonial troops forced the population to deliver rubber and ivory; those who failed to meet the quotas were flogged, mutilated or killed, and entire villages were burned down. Through violence, forced labor, hunger and disease, several million people are estimated to have died. Reports by the British consul Roger Casement and the campaign of Edmund Morel caused an international scandal, so that Belgium took over the colony in 1908.

title: Carl Benz Builds the First Automobile
summary: In Mannheim, Carl Benz files a patent for a three-wheeled vehicle with a gasoline engine.
text: On 29 January 1886 Carl Benz received the patent for his vehicle powered by a gas engine, the first practical car with an internal combustion engine; at almost the same time Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach built a motor carriage in Cannstatt. In August 1888 Bertha Benz drove with her sons from Mannheim to Pforzheim without her husband's knowledge, the first long-distance journey by automobile, and proved that it was suitable for everyday use. The car stood for the second Industrial Revolution, in which electricity, chemistry and the internal combustion engine reinvented the technology of daily life. With Ford's assembly line it became a mass product from 1913 onward.

title: Women's Suffrage in New Zealand
summary: New Zealand becomes the first country in the world to grant all women the right to vote in national elections.
text: In 1893 the women's rights campaigner Kate Sheppard and her fellow activists collected almost 32,000 signatures for a petition, at the time a quarter of all adult women in New Zealand. On 19 September 1893 the governor signed the electoral law, and as early as November women, among them Maori women, voted for parliament for the first time. South Australia followed in 1894, and Finland in 1906 as the first European country; in Germany and Britain it took until 1918. The success in New Zealand became a model for the women's movement around the world.

title: Boxer Rebellion in China
summary: An uprising against foreigners and Christians in China is put down jointly by eight powers.
text: The secret society known as the Boxers turned against missionaries, railways and the growing control of the great powers over China. In June 1900, after the German envoy had been murdered, Boxers and imperial troops besieged the legation quarter in Beijing for 55 days. An expeditionary force from eight states, among them Japan, Russia, Britain, the United States and Germany, captured Beijing and plundered the city; Emperor William II had urged the German troops to show no mercy in his Hun speech. The Boxer Protocol of 1901 forced China to pay enormous reparations and accelerated the decline of the Qing dynasty, which was overthrown in 1911.

title: First Powered Flight by the Wright Brothers
summary: Orville and Wilbur Wright achieve the first controlled powered flight at Kitty Hawk.
text: On 17 December 1903 Orville Wright lifted off from the beach at Kitty Hawk in North Carolina for twelve seconds in the Flyer he had built himself. The two bicycle mechanics had experimented with gliders for years and had developed a system for controlling the aircraft about all three axes. Aircraft were already used militarily in the First World War, and within a few decades aviation fundamentally changed both travel and warfare.

title: Genocide of the Herero and Nama
summary: German colonial troops destroy a large part of the Herero and Nama in German South West Africa.
text: After the seizure of their land and the loss of their rights, the Herero rose up in January 1904 against German colonial rule in what is now Namibia. After the Battle of Waterberg, General Lothar von Trotha drove them into the waterless Omaheke Desert and ordered that every Herero be shot. Survivors, and later the Nama who had also risen up, were forced into labor in concentration camps. Up to 80 percent of the Herero and half of the Nama lost their lives; in 2021 the Federal Republic of Germany recognized the crimes as genocide.

title: First Automobile Assembly Line at Ford
summary: Henry Ford introduces the moving assembly line in Detroit for production of the Model T.
text: At the Highland Park plant, Henry Ford had the chassis of the Model T pulled past the workers on a rope, each of them performing just one operation. The time needed to assemble a car fell from more than twelve hours to about one and a half. The car became so cheap that workers too could afford one. Assembly-line production became the model for mass production in the 20th century.

title: Assassination in Sarajevo
summary: The murder of the Austrian heir to the throne, Franz Ferdinand, triggers the First World War.
text: On 28 June 1914 the Serbian nationalist Gavrilo Princip shot dead the heir to the throne, Franz Ferdinand, and his wife Sophie in Sarajevo. Backed by Germany, Austria-Hungary issued an ultimatum to Serbia and declared war on 28 July. Through the alliances between Russia and Serbia, France and Russia, and Britain and Belgium, the conflict widened into a European war within a week. The July Crisis is regarded as an example of how the automatic workings of alliances and misjudgments can lead to a great war that nobody wanted.

title: Battle of the Marne and the Beginning of Trench Warfare
summary: The German advance on Paris is halted at the Marne; the Western Front freezes into trench warfare for four years.
text: According to the Schlieffen Plan, the German army was to defeat France in six weeks by advancing through Belgium, before Russia was fully mobilized in the east. At the beginning of September 1914 German troops stood 40 kilometers from Paris, but from 5 to 12 September French and British forces threw them back in the Battle of the Marne, with Parisian taxis bringing reinforcements to the front. In the east Hindenburg and Ludendorff had won at Tannenberg, but the chance of a quick victory in the west had been lost. After a race to the sea, both sides dug into trenches by the end of the year along 700 kilometers from the North Sea to the Swiss border, and machine guns, barbed wire and artillery turned every attack into mass death.

title: Battle of Gallipoli
summary: The Allied landing at the Dardanelles fails against the Ottoman defense and costs more than 100,000 lives.
text: In order to force the Ottoman Empire out of the war and open a sea route to Russia, British and French ships attempted in the spring of 1915 to force the straits of the Dardanelles. When this failed, British, French, Australian and New Zealand troops landed on the Gallipoli peninsula on 25 April 1915. The Ottoman defenders, among them Colonel Mustafa Kemal, held the heights, and the fighting froze as it had on the Western Front. In January 1916 the Allies evacuated the peninsula; more than 100,000 soldiers on both sides were dead. In Australia and New Zealand 25 April is still commemorated today as Anzac Day, and for Turkey the victory became a founding myth.

title: Armenian Genocide
summary: The Young Turk government has the Armenian population of the Ottoman Empire deported and murdered.
text: On 24 April 1915 the government of the Committee of Union and Progress had hundreds of Armenian intellectuals and politicians arrested in Constantinople, and most of them were later killed. The Armenian communities of Anatolia were then sent on death marches into the Syrian desert on the pretext of wartime security; men were shot, while women, children and the elderly died of hunger, thirst and violence or in camps near Deir ez-Zor. Estimates put the number of dead at around one million, and there were also mass killings of Assyrians and Greeks. The allied German Empire was informed through its diplomats and officers but did not intervene. The historian Raphael Lemkin later coined the term genocide with this crime and the Holocaust in mind; the German Bundestag recognized the genocide in 2016, while Turkey disputes the term to this day.

title: Battle of Verdun
summary: Ten months of industrialized battle over the French fortress claim more than 700,000 dead and wounded.
text: In February 1916 the German high command attacked the fortress of Verdun in order to bleed the French army dry in a battle of attrition. Both sides fired millions of shells onto a few square kilometers of ground; villages disappeared completely. When the fighting ended in December, the front ran almost unchanged. Verdun became a symbol of the futility of trench warfare and later of Franco-German reconciliation.

title: Balfour Declaration
summary: Britain promises the Jews a national home in Palestine and thereby lays the ground for the Middle East conflict.
text: On 2 November 1917 the British foreign secretary Arthur Balfour stated in a letter to Lord Rothschild that the government viewed with favor the establishment of a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine, without prejudice to the rights of the non-Jewish communities living there. The pledge was intended to win the Zionist movement and the Jewish public in the United States and Russia over to the war effort. At the same time Britain had held out the prospect of a state of their own to the Arabs in return for their revolt against the Ottomans, and in the Sykes-Picot Agreement had secretly divided the Middle East into spheres of influence with France. In 1920 Britain received the League of Nations mandate over Palestine; growing Jewish immigration and the resistance of the Arab population led to the first violent clashes in the 1920s and 1930s.

title: Entry of the United States into the War
summary: After the unrestricted submarine warfare, the United States declares war on Germany.
text: President Woodrow Wilson had kept the United States out of the war for years. When Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare in February 1917 and the Zimmermann Telegram revealed a German offer of alliance to Mexico, Congress declared war on 6 April 1917. More than two million American soldiers and the industrial strength of the United States tipped the balance of power in favor of the Entente.

title: Russian Revolution
summary: The tsar is overthrown, and in October the Bolsheviks under Lenin seize power.
text: Hunger, war weariness and strikes forced Tsar Nicholas II to abdicate in March 1917; a provisional government, however, continued the war. Lenin, whom the German government allowed to travel from exile in Switzerland to Russia, demanded peace, land and all power to the soviets. In November the Bolsheviks overthrew the government in Petrograd. There followed the peace of Brest-Litovsk, a bloody civil war and, in 1922, the founding of the Soviet Union.

title: November Revolution in Germany
summary: Mutinying sailors and striking workers overthrow the monarchy; Germany becomes a republic and introduces women's suffrage.
text: When the naval command wanted to send the fleet out at the end of October 1918 for a final battle against England, the sailors in Wilhelmshaven and Kiel refused the order. Within a few days the revolt spread across the whole empire: workers' and soldiers' councils took power in the cities, the princes abdicated, and on 9 November Philipp Scheidemann proclaimed the republic in Berlin, while a few hours later Karl Liebknecht proclaimed a socialist republic. Friedrich Ebert took over the government as the Council of People's Deputies, which on 12 November announced the eight-hour day and the right to vote for women. The labor movement broke apart over the question of whether Germany should become a parliamentary democracy or a council republic; in January 1919 the government had the Spartacist uprising crushed by Freikorps units, and Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht were murdered.

title: Spanish Flu
summary: A worldwide influenza pandemic claims more lives than the First World War.
text: In the spring of 1918 a new influenza appeared in military camps in the United States and on the Western Front, spreading across the whole world with troop transports. It got its name because the newspapers of neutral Spain, free of wartime censorship, reported on the disease in detail. In a second, far deadlier wave in the autumn of 1918, unusually many young adults died of pneumonia within a few days. By 1920 about a third of the world's population had been infected, and at least 20 to 50 million people died, particularly many of them in India. Schools, theaters and churches were closed and masks were made compulsory, but without antibiotics and vaccines medicine remained largely powerless.

title: Armistice of Compiègne
summary: On 11 November 1918 the guns fall silent on the Western Front; the First World War is over.
text: After the failure of the German spring offensive and the collapse of its allies, the Supreme Army Command itself called for an armistice in the autumn of 1918. In Germany sailors mutinied, workers' and soldiers' councils took power, and on 9 November the republic was proclaimed; William II fled to the Netherlands. In a railway carriage in the forest of Compiègne the German delegation signed the harsh conditions set by the Allies. They came into force at 11 o'clock on 11 November.

title: Founding of the Bauhaus
summary: Walter Gropius founds a school in Weimar that links art, craft and industry and establishes modern design.
text: In April 1919 the architect Walter Gropius merged the academy of art and the school of arts and crafts in Weimar into the Staatliches Bauhaus, whose manifesto set out the aim of bringing all the arts together under the roof of building. Teachers such as Wassily Kandinsky, Paul Klee, Lyonel Feininger and László Moholy-Nagy, and workshop masters such as the weaver Gunta Stölzl and the metal designer Marianne Brandt, designed furniture, lamps, tableware and typefaces for industrial mass production. In 1925 the school moved into the building in Dessau designed by Gropius, and in 1932 to Berlin, where the National Socialists closed it in 1933. Many members of the Bauhaus emigrated and carried the school's ideas to the United States, to Israel and around the world; the Bauhaus became a symbol of the Golden Twenties and of modernism.

title: National Assembly and the Weimar Constitution
summary: The first German democracy receives its constitution; for the first time women vote and enter parliament.
text: On 19 January 1919 Germans elected a constituent national assembly, in which women took part as voters and candidates for the first time; 37 of them were elected. Because there was unrest in Berlin, the parliament met in the National Theatre in Weimar, elected Friedrich Ebert as Reich President and on 19 February heard Marie Juchacz give the first speech by a woman in a German parliament. The constitution signed on 11 August 1919 made Germany a parliamentary republic with universal suffrage from the age of 20, fundamental rights, referendums and a strong, directly elected Reich President. Article 48 on emergency decrees and the system of pure proportional representation, which brought many small parties into parliament, later proved to be weak points that the opponents of the republic exploited.

title: Treaty of Versailles
summary: The peace treaty imposes territorial losses, disarmament, reparations and war guilt on Germany.
text: The victorious powers negotiated the treaty without German participation and forced the government of the young Weimar Republic to sign it on 28 June 1919. Germany lost Alsace-Lorraine, large parts of West Prussia and Posen as well as all its colonies, was allowed to maintain an army of only 100,000 men and had to pay reparations. Article 231 assigned responsibility for the war to Germany and its allies. Nationalists used the treaty as a dictated peace of shame in their propaganda against the republic.

title: Founding of the League of Nations
summary: The first worldwide organization for securing peace begins its work in Geneva.
text: The League of Nations went back to Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points and was intended to resolve conflicts through negotiation, arbitration and joint sanctions. The United States of all countries never joined, because the Senate rejected the treaty; Germany was admitted only in 1926 and the Soviet Union in 1934. Without troops of its own, the League was unable to prevent the acts of aggression by Japan, Italy and Germany in the 1930s. Its subsidiary organizations for labor, health and refugees lived on in the United Nations.

title: Founding of the Republic of Turkey
summary: The secular Republic of Turkey emerges under Mustafa Kemal from the collapsed Ottoman Empire.
text: The Ottoman Empire had lost the war at Germany's side and was to be largely partitioned under the Treaty of Sèvres. Mustafa Kemal organized the resistance, defeated the Greek troops in Anatolia and secured the present-day borders in the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923. On 29 October 1923 the republic was proclaimed. Kemal abolished the sultanate and the caliphate, separated religion and state, and introduced the Latin alphabet and women's suffrage.

title: The Crisis Year 1923: Occupation of the Ruhr, Hyperinflation and the Hitler Putsch
summary: The mark becomes worthless, France occupies the Ruhr region, and in Munich Hitler attempts a coup.
text: When Germany fell behind with its reparation deliveries, French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr region in January 1923. The Reich government called for passive resistance and paid the striking workers with freshly printed money, which drove the inflation that had been running since the war to immeasurable heights: in November one dollar cost 4.2 trillion marks, a loaf of bread cost billions, and wages were paid out daily so that they could still be spent on the same day. Gustav Stresemann, chancellor since August, broke off the struggle in the Ruhr and on 15 November introduced the Rentenmark, which stabilized the currency. A few days earlier, on 8 and 9 November, Adolf Hitler had attempted a putsch in Munich together with Erich Ludendorff, which ended in a hail of police bullets in front of the Feldherrnhalle; Hitler used the trial as a stage and wrote his book Mein Kampf in prison.

title: Great Depression
summary: The stock market crash in New York plunges the world into the most severe economic crisis of modern times.
text: On 24 October 1929, Black Thursday, share prices collapsed on the New York stock exchange. Banks went bankrupt, American loans were withdrawn from Europe, and world trade shrank by more than half. In the United States one in four of the workforce was unemployed in 1933, and in Germany more than six million people were out of work. The hardship undermined confidence in democracy and contributed decisively to the rise of the National Socialists.

title: Gandhi's Salt March
summary: With a march of 385 kilometers to the sea, Gandhi breaks the British salt monopoly and makes nonviolent resistance known throughout the world.
text: The British salt monopoly forbade Indians to produce salt themselves and placed a tax on this basic foodstuff that hit the poor hardest. On 12 March 1930 Mohandas Gandhi set out from his ashram near Ahmedabad with 78 followers; after 24 days he reached the village of Dandi on the Arabian Sea accompanied by tens of thousands of people and there, on 6 April, demonstratively picked up a handful of salt. All over the country people now boiled salt, boycotted British goods and resigned from public office; the colonial power arrested more than 60,000 people, Gandhi himself among them. The images of police beating peaceful demonstrators went around the world and weakened the moral authority of the empire. The march became a model for nonviolent movements right up to Martin Luther King.

title: Book Burning
summary: In Berlin and twenty other university towns, students throw the works of Jewish, left-wing and pacifist authors into the fire.
text: In the spring of 1933 the National Socialist German Students' League called for a campaign against the un-German spirit and ransacked libraries and bookshops. On 10 May 1933 students and SA men burned tens of thousands of books by torchlight on the Opernplatz in Berlin, while propaganda minister Joseph Goebbels proclaimed the end of Jewish intellectualism; similar fires burned in Bonn, Frankfurt, Munich, Dresden and many other cities. Among those affected were Heinrich and Thomas Mann, Erich Kästner, who watched the burning of his own books from the crowd, Kurt Tucholsky, Erich Maria Remarque, Sigmund Freud, Karl Marx and Bertolt Brecht. More than a hundred years earlier Heinrich Heine, whose works also burned, had written that where books are burned, in the end people will be burned too. The burning stood at the beginning of a cultural policy that drove modern literature out of Germany.

title: National Socialist Seizure of Power
summary: Hitler becomes chancellor and establishes a dictatorship within a few months.
text: On 30 January 1933 Reich President Hindenburg appointed Hitler chancellor of a coalition in which conservative politicians believed they could control him. After the Reichstag fire, the emergency decree of 28 February suspended fundamental rights, and the Enabling Act of 23 March transferred legislative power to the government. By the summer all other parties had been banned, the trade unions smashed and the first concentration camps set up. After Hindenburg's death in 1934, Hitler combined the offices of chancellor and president as Führer and Reich Chancellor.

title: Reichstag Fire and Enabling Act
summary: The burning of the Reichstag provides the pretext for abolishing fundamental rights; the Enabling Act strips parliament of its power.
text: On the night of 27 February 1933 the Reichstag building stood in flames; at the scene the Dutch council communist Marinus van der Lubbe was arrested, who claimed to have acted alone. That same night the government declared the fire to be the signal for a communist uprising, and as early as 28 February the Reichstag Fire Decree suspended freedom of opinion, of the press and of assembly as well as protection against arbitrary arrest. Thousands of communists and social democrats were arrested, and the election of 5 March took place under terror. On 23 March, in the Kroll Opera House surrounded by the SA, the Reichstag approved the Enabling Act by 444 votes to 94, allowing the government to issue laws without parliament and without the constitution; only the SPD voted against, and its chairman Otto Wels declared that freedom and life could be taken from them, but not their honor. The KPD deputies had already been arrested or had gone into hiding.

title: The Long March
summary: China's communists escape encirclement by Chiang Kai-shek in a year-long retreat that brings Mao Zedong to the head of the party.
text: From 1927 onward Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist Chinese government fought the communists, who had established a soviet republic of their own in the southern Chinese province of Jiangxi. When the fifth encirclement campaign threatened to crush the Red Army in the autumn of 1934, some 86,000 soldiers and cadres broke out to the west. Crossing rivers, swamps and snow-covered mountains, they covered several thousand kilometers in one year, constantly pursued by government troops and local warlords; only a few thousand reached the region around Yan'an in northern China in October 1935. At the Zunyi Conference in January 1935 Mao Zedong had taken over the leadership. The Long March became a founding myth of the People's Republic, and after the Xi'an Incident in 1936 Chiang and the communists had to form a united front against Japan.

title: Nuremberg Laws
summary: The racial laws make Jews second-class citizens and prohibit marriages with non-Jews.
text: At the party rally in Nuremberg on 15 September 1935, the Reichstag proclaimed the Reich Citizenship Law and the Law for the Protection of German Blood and German Honor. Jews lost their full civil rights, and marriages and relationships between Jews and non-Jews were made punishable. Who counted as a Jew was decided by the authorities on the basis of the origin of the grandparents, not on the basis of faith. The laws created the legal basis for the exclusion, expropriation and later deportation of the Jews.

title: Great Purge in the Soviet Union
summary: In show trials and mass operations Stalin has hundreds of thousands shot as alleged enemies of the people.
text: After the murder of the Leningrad party leader Sergei Kirov in December 1934, Stalin used the fear of conspiracies to destroy every actual or possible opposition. In three Moscow show trials between 1936 and 1938, old companions of Lenin such as Zinoviev, Kamenev and Bukharin confessed under torture to invented crimes and were shot; Trotsky, who had been driven into exile, was also condemned in absentia and murdered in Mexico in 1940. In 1937 Stalin had the leadership of the Red Army around Marshal Tukhachevsky executed. In the mass operations of the NKVD secret police under Nikolai Yezhov, around 750,000 people were shot according to quotas in 1937 and 1938, and well over a million were deported to the camps of the Gulag. The purge destroyed the country's leading stratum and weakened the army shortly before the German attack.

title: Spanish Civil War
summary: Nationalists under Franco overthrow the Spanish republic with German and Italian help.
text: In July 1936 parts of the military under General Francisco Franco rose against the elected government of the Popular Front. Germany and Italy sent aircraft and troops, the Soviet Union supported the republic, and volunteers from all over the world fought in the International Brigades. The destruction of the Basque town of Guernica by the German Condor Legion in 1937 became a symbol of aerial warfare against civilians. Franco's victory in April 1939 established a dictatorship that lasted until 1975.

title: Nanking Massacre
summary: After capturing the Chinese capital, Japanese troops commit mass murder and mass rape for weeks on end.
text: Since the Marco Polo Bridge Incident in July 1937 Japan had waged open war against China, and after heavy fighting around Shanghai it took the capital Nanking on 13 December 1937. Over the following six weeks Japanese soldiers shot, stabbed and drowned tens of thousands of captured soldiers and civilians, raped tens of thousands of women and girls, and looted and burned the city. The International Military Tribunal for the Far East assumed more than 200,000 dead, and China gives the figure of 300,000; historians dispute the number, but not the crime. A group of foreigners around the German Siemens representative John Rabe set up a safety zone in which around 200,000 people found protection. The massacre still burdens relations between China and Japan today, because Japanese nationalists play it down or deny it.

title: Munich Agreement
summary: Britain and France hand Hitler the Sudetenland in order to avoid war; Czechoslovakia is not consulted.
text: After the annexation of Austria in March 1938, Hitler demanded the cession of the Sudetenland, the border regions of Czechoslovakia inhabited by around three million Germans, and threatened war. The British prime minister Neville Chamberlain flew to Germany three times to negotiate, and during the night of 30 September 1938 Hitler, Mussolini, Chamberlain and the French prime minister Daladier signed the agreement in Munich, which laid down that the cession was to take place within ten days. The Czechoslovak government, allied with France, had to give in and lost its border fortifications. In London people cheered Chamberlain, who promised peace for our time; Winston Churchill called the agreement a total defeat. In March 1939 the Wehrmacht occupied the remainder of the Czech lands and demonstrated that the policy of appeasement had failed.

title: November Pogroms
summary: During the night of 9 to 10 November, synagogues burn throughout the Reich and Jewish businesses are destroyed.
text: The pretext was the assassination of a German diplomat in Paris by a young Jew. On Goebbels's instructions, the SA and SS destroyed more than 1,400 synagogues and thousands of businesses and homes, and hundreds of people were killed. Around 30,000 Jewish men were deported to concentration camps. The victims had to pay for the damage themselves and to raise an atonement payment of one billion reichsmarks. The pogroms marked the transition from the removal of rights to open violence.

title: Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact
summary: The mortal enemies Germany and the Soviet Union conclude a non-aggression pact and secretly divide Eastern Europe between them.
text: On 23 August 1939 the foreign ministers Joachim von Ribbentrop and Vyacheslav Molotov signed a non-aggression treaty in Moscow that took the world by surprise, because National Socialism and communism had fought each other for years as arch-enemies. A secret additional protocol divided Poland along the rivers Narew, Vistula and San and assigned Finland, Estonia, Latvia and Bessarabia to the Soviet sphere of interest and Lithuania initially to the German one. Hitler thereby had a free hand for the attack on Poland, while Stalin gained time and territory. In September 1939 the Soviet Union occupied eastern Poland, in the spring of 1940 had around 22,000 Polish officers and officials shot at Katyn, waged war against Finland and annexed the Baltic states in 1940. The Soviet Union denied the existence of the protocol until 1989.

title: Invasion of Poland and the Outbreak of War
summary: With the German attack on Poland on 1 September 1939 the Second World War begins.
text: One week after the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, which in a secret additional protocol divided Poland between Germany and the Soviet Union, the Wehrmacht attacked without a declaration of war. Britain and France declared war on Germany on 3 September, but were unable to help Poland. On 17 September the Red Army marched in from the east; by the beginning of October Poland was defeated. In the occupied territories the mass shootings of the Polish leading class and the persecution of the Jews began at once.

title: Battle of Britain
summary: The Royal Air Force prevents the Luftwaffe from gaining air supremacy and thereby prevents the German invasion of Britain.
text: After the fall of France, Britain stood alone, and Hitler had a landing on the English coast prepared, for which the Royal Air Force first had to be eliminated. From July to October 1940 the Luftwaffe attacked ports, airfields and radar stations, but the British Spitfire and Hurricane fighters, guided by the radar system and the ground control of Fighter Command, inflicted heavier losses on the attackers than they suffered themselves; pilots from Poland, Czechoslovakia, Canada and other countries fought alongside them. When the Luftwaffe switched in September to night attacks on London and other cities, the Blitz, this gave the Royal Air Force the decisive respite. On 17 September Hitler postponed the invasion indefinitely; by May 1941 more than 40,000 British civilians had died in the bombing war. Churchill thanked the pilots with the words that never was so much owed by so many to so few.

title: Western Campaign and the Fall of France
summary: In six weeks the Wehrmacht defeats the Netherlands, Belgium and France; de Gaulle calls for resistance from London.
text: On 10 May 1940 the Wehrmacht attacked the neutral Netherlands and Belgium and, with its panzer divisions, among them the 7th Panzer Division led by Erwin Rommel, pushed unexpectedly through the wooded Ardennes, where the Allies did not expect an attack. Within a week the Germans reached the Channel coast and cut off the British and French armies in Belgium; around 338,000 soldiers were evacuated across the Channel at Dunkirk. Paris fell on 14 June, and on 22 June the new government under Marshal Pétain signed the capitulation in the same railway carriage at Compiègne in which the armistice had been sealed in 1918; northern France was occupied, and in the south the Vichy regime arose, which collaborated with Germany. On 18 June General Charles de Gaulle called on the French over the BBC to continue the fight; out of his Free France and the networks of the Résistance inside the country there grew by 1944 a resistance movement that carried out sabotage, hid the persecuted and supplied the Allies with information.

title: Attack on the Soviet Union
summary: With Operation Barbarossa the German war of annihilation in the east begins on 22 June 1941.
text: More than three million German and allied soldiers crossed the border into the Soviet Union; it was the largest attack in military history. The aim was the conquest of living space and the destruction of Bolshevism. Behind the front, Einsatzgruppen shot hundreds of thousands of Jews, Soviet prisoners of war were left to starve to death in their millions, and the siege of Leningrad cost more than a million civilians their lives. The advance came to a halt before Moscow in December 1941.

title: Attack on Pearl Harbor
summary: Japan launches a surprise attack on the American Pacific Fleet in Hawaii; the United States enters the war.
text: On 7 December 1941 Japanese carrier aircraft sank or damaged eight battleships and killed more than 2,400 Americans. Japan wanted to secure its expansion in Southeast Asia after the United States had imposed an oil embargo. On the following day Congress declared war on Japan, and a few days later Germany and Italy declared war on the United States. With that the war had definitively become a world war, and the industrial superiority of the United States began to take effect.

title: Battle of Midway
summary: The US Navy sinks four Japanese aircraft carriers and halts Japanese expansion in the Pacific.
text: Six months after Pearl Harbor, Admiral Yamamoto sought to force the American fleet into a decisive battle by attacking the atoll of Midway. American codebreakers, however, had partly deciphered the Japanese naval code, so that Admiral Nimitz was able to position his three carriers in ambush. On 4 June 1942 American dive bombers hit the Japanese carriers at the very moment when their aircraft were being refueled and armed on deck; Akagi, Kaga, Soryu and Hiryu sank, and the United States lost the Yorktown. Japan lost the core of its carrier fleet and hundreds of experienced pilots and was never able to replace these losses, while American shipyards delivered new ships every month. From Guadalcanal onward in August 1942 the United States went on the offensive in the Pacific.

title: Battle of El Alamein
summary: The British Eighth Army defeats Rommel's panzer army in Egypt and turns the war in North Africa.
text: Since 1941 the German Afrika Korps under Erwin Rommel and Italian troops had been fighting the British for Libya and for access to the Suez Canal and the oil fields of the Middle East. In the summer of 1942, after the capture of Tobruk, Rommel stood only 100 kilometers from Alexandria, but his supply lines were overextended, and Allied aircraft and submarines sank his tankers in the Mediterranean. The new British commander Bernard Montgomery attacked on 23 October 1942 with roughly twice the strength in soldiers, tanks and aircraft, including troops from Australia, New Zealand, India and South Africa; after twelve days the German-Italian front broke, and Rommel withdrew to the west in defiance of an order from Hitler to hold. A few days later American and British troops landed in Morocco and Algeria; in May 1943 around 250,000 Axis soldiers surrendered in Tunisia. Churchill called El Alamein the end of the beginning.

title: Battle of Stalingrad
summary: The encirclement and destruction of the Sixth Army on the Volga is regarded as the turning point of the war in Europe.
text: In the summer of 1942 the Wehrmacht advanced as far as the Volga and fought in bitter street battles for the city of Stalingrad. In November the Red Army encircled the German troops; Hitler forbade a breakout. After hunger, cold and fighting, the remnants of the Sixth Army surrendered on 2 February 1943. About 150,000 German soldiers had been killed and around 90,000 were taken prisoner, of whom only about 6,000 returned. After that the Wehrmacht was permanently on the defensive in the east.

title: Wannsee Conference
summary: Senior officials and SS leaders coordinate the deportation and murder of all European Jews.
text: On 20 January 1942 fifteen representatives of the SS, the party and the ministries met under the chairmanship of Reinhard Heydrich in a villa on the Wannsee in Berlin. The conference did not decide on the genocide, since mass murder had already been under way for months, but organized the cooperation of the authorities in the so-called Final Solution of the Jewish Question. The minutes named eleven million Jews across the whole of Europe as the target group. In the months that followed, the deportations to the extermination camps of Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka and Auschwitz-Birkenau began.

title: Warsaw Ghetto Uprising
summary: The last inhabitants of the ghetto put up armed resistance to the SS for almost four weeks, choosing to fight rather than be deported.
text: In the Warsaw ghetto, which the German occupation had sealed off with a wall in 1940, more than 400,000 people lived crammed into the narrowest of spaces, and tens of thousands of them died of hunger and disease. Between July and September 1942 the SS deported about 265,000 inhabitants to the Treblinka extermination camp. The remaining 60,000 or so now knew what deportation meant; young people joined together in the Jewish Combat Organization under the 24-year-old Mordechai Anielewicz and in the Jewish Military Union, laboriously procuring pistols and homemade firebombs. When the SS moved in on 19 April 1943 for the final clearance, it came under fire and had to withdraw. The SS commander Jürgen Stroop thereupon had the ghetto burned down and blown up house by house; on 8 May Anielewicz and his comrades died in the bunker on Miła Street, and on 16 May, after the demolition of the Great Synagogue, Stroop reported that the ghetto no longer existed. About 7,000 people had died in the fighting, and the survivors were deported to Treblinka and Majdanek. The uprising was the first large armed revolt in an occupied city and became a symbol of Jewish resistance.

title: Assassination Attempt of 20 July 1944
summary: Stauffenberg's bomb misses Hitler, the coup fails, and the regime takes revenge with hundreds of executions.
text: A circle of officers, diplomats, trade unionists and politicians had been planning for years to remove Hitler and end the war before Germany was completely destroyed. On 20 July 1944 Colonel Claus Schenk Graf von Stauffenberg detonated a bomb in a briefcase during a situation conference at the Wolf's Lair headquarters in East Prussia. Four men died, but Hitler was only slightly injured because the briefcase had been pushed behind a massive table support. Stauffenberg flew to Berlin and, with his fellow conspirators in the Bendlerblock, set in motion the Valkyrie plan, under which the Replacement Army was to take power; when word spread that Hitler had survived, the coup collapsed. Stauffenberg, Friedrich Olbricht, Albrecht Mertz von Quirnheim and Werner von Haeften were shot in the courtyard that same night. In the following months the People's Court under Roland Freisler sentenced around 200 people to death, among them Helmuth James von Moltke, Carl Goerdeler and Julius Leber; their relatives were taken into kin liability detention. Today 20 July is regarded as a symbol of the fact that even among the leading class of the Reich there were people who placed their conscience above obedience.

title: D-Day in Normandy
summary: With the largest landing operation in history, the Western Allies open the second front in France.
text: On 6 June 1944 more than 150,000 American, British and Canadian soldiers landed on five stretches of beach in Normandy, supported by almost 7,000 ships and 11,000 aircraft. Despite heavy losses, above all at Omaha Beach, a bridgehead was successfully established. By the end of August Paris had been liberated, and the Wehrmacht had to withdraw to the German border. At the same time the Soviet summer offensive smashed the German Army Group Centre.

title: Atomic Bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki
summary: The United States uses nuclear weapons for the first time; Japan surrenders and the Second World War is over.
text: On 6 August 1945 the atomic bomb Little Boy destroyed the city of Hiroshima, and on 9 August Fat Man struck Nagasaki. By the end of 1945 more than 200,000 people had died from the explosion, the fires and the radiation. President Truman wanted to avoid a costly invasion of Japan; at the same time the Soviet Union declared war on Japan. On 15 August Emperor Hirohito announced the surrender, which was signed on 2 September. The atomic age had begun.

title: Liberation of Auschwitz
summary: Soviet soldiers reach the largest extermination camp of the National Socialists on 27 January 1945.
text: At Auschwitz-Birkenau in occupied Poland the SS had murdered more than 1.1 million people between 1940 and 1945, among them around one million Jews, as well as Poles, Sinti and Roma and Soviet prisoners of war. Shortly before the liberation the SS drove about 60,000 prisoners westward on death marches; the soldiers of the Red Army found around 7,000 exhausted survivors, among them many children. Today 27 January is the international day of remembrance for the victims of the Holocaust.

title: Founding of the United Nations
summary: 51 states sign the Charter of the United Nations in San Francisco.
text: While the war was still going on, the Allies had prepared a new world organization that was to be stronger than the failed League of Nations. The charter was signed on 26 June 1945 and came into force on 24 October. The Security Council, with its five permanent members the United States, the Soviet Union, Britain, France and China, received the right to decide on sanctions and military operations. In 1948 the General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

title: Surrender of Germany
summary: With the unconditional surrender of the Wehrmacht on 8 May 1945 the war in Europe comes to an end.
text: After the Red Army had captured Berlin and Hitler had taken his own life in the bunker of the Reich Chancellery on 30 April, the leadership of the Wehrmacht signed the unconditional surrender on 7 May in Reims and on 8 May in Berlin-Karlshorst. Germany was divided into four occupation zones, and the major war criminals were indicted before the Nuremberg tribunal. In Germany today 8 May is understood as the day of liberation from National Socialism.

title: Nuremberg Trials
summary: For the first time the leaders of a state have to answer before an international court for waging a war of aggression and for crimes against humanity.
text: In the summer of 1945 the four victorious powers agreed not to shoot those chiefly responsible for the Nazi regime by summary justice, but to charge them in proceedings under the rule of law. From 20 November 1945 to 1 October 1946 the International Military Tribunal sat in the Palace of Justice in Nuremberg and tried 24 defendants, among them Hermann Göring, Rudolf Hess, Joachim von Ribbentrop and Albert Speer, for conspiracy, crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity. The evidence consisted above all of the perpetrators' own files, together with films from the liberated camps and testimony from survivors; the objection that they had only been following orders was not accepted as an excuse. Twelve defendants were sentenced to death, Göring escaped execution by taking poison, and three were acquitted. In twelve subsequent trials up to 1949, doctors, lawyers, industrialists, diplomats and commanders of the Einsatzgruppen stood before American courts, and in Tokyo a parallel tribunal tried the Japanese leadership. The Nuremberg Principles became the foundation of international criminal law and of the International Criminal Court.

title: Independence of India and Pakistan
summary: British India becomes independent and is divided into the states of India and Pakistan.
text: After decades of nonviolent resistance under Mahatma Gandhi, Britain released its most important colony into independence on 15 August 1947. Because Hindus and Muslims could not agree on a common state, the country was divided into predominantly Hindu India and Muslim Pakistan. Up to 15 million people fled across the new borders, and hundreds of thousands died in massacres. The dispute over Kashmir still burdens relations between the two nuclear powers today.

title: Berlin Airlift
summary: After the Soviet blockade of West Berlin, the Western powers supply the city from the air for almost a year.
text: When the Western powers introduced the deutschmark in their zones in June 1948, the Soviet Union closed all roads, railways and waterways to West Berlin in order to push the Western Allies out of the city. The United States and Britain thereupon set up an airlift: in almost 280,000 flights the raisin bombers brought around 2.3 million tons of coal, food and medicine to the roughly two million Berliners. On 12 May 1949 Stalin lifted the blockade. The airlift turned the occupiers into protectors in the eyes of many Germans, led to the founding of NATO in 1949 and accelerated the emergence of the Federal Republic and the GDR in the same year.

title: Founding of Israel
summary: David Ben-Gurion proclaims the State of Israel; the first Arab-Israeli war begins.
text: In 1947 the United Nations had decided to partition the British mandate territory of Palestine into a Jewish and an Arab state. On 14 May 1948 Ben-Gurion proclaimed the independence of Israel, which after the Holocaust offered a home to many survivors. The neighboring Arab states attacked at once, Israel held its ground and enlarged its territory. Around 700,000 Palestinians fled or were driven out; the refugee question and the borders remain at the heart of the Middle East conflict to this day.

title: Proclamation of the People's Republic of China
summary: After victory in the civil war, Mao Zedong proclaims the People's Republic in Beijing.
text: The civil war between Mao's communists and the nationalists under Chiang Kai-shek ended in 1949 with the withdrawal of the nationalists to Taiwan. On 1 October Mao proclaimed the founding of the People's Republic from the Gate of Heavenly Peace. The communists distributed the land to the peasants and built up a planned economy on the Soviet model. Mao's campaigns such as the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution later cost millions of people their lives.

title: Korean War
summary: North Korea's attack on the South leads to the first hot war of the Cold War, with millions of dead.
text: In 1945 Korea had been divided along the 38th parallel into a Soviet and an American zone, out of which two hostile states emerged. On 25 June 1950 communist North Korea attacked the South with Stalin's approval; the United Nations, from whose Security Council the Soviet Union was absent at the time, sent troops under American command. After the landing at Incheon the UN forces advanced as far as the Chinese border, whereupon China intervened with hundreds of thousands of soldiers. The armistice of 1953 restored the old border; a peace treaty was never concluded. Around three million people died, and Korea remains divided to this day.

title: Bandung Conference
summary: 29 Asian and African states meet in Indonesia and call for a path of their own between the blocs.
text: At the invitation of Indonesia, India, Pakistan, Burma and Ceylon, representatives of 29 states, together representing more than half of the world's population, came together in Bandung in April 1955. Jawaharlal Nehru, Sukarno, Gamal Abdel Nasser and China's prime minister Zhou Enlai condemned colonialism and racism, called for respect for sovereignty and rejected alignment with the military blocs. For the first time the conference gave the decolonized countries a common voice in world politics. Out of it grew the Non-Aligned Movement in Belgrade in 1961, which still exists today.

title: Montgomery Bus Boycott
summary: The arrest of Rosa Parks sets off a boycott lasting 381 days and makes Martin Luther King the leader of the civil rights movement.
text: On 1 December 1955 the seamstress Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat on a bus to a white passenger in Montgomery, Alabama, and was arrested. The city's black community thereupon decided to stop using the buses; for more than a year tens of thousands walked or organized car pools. The 26-year-old pastor Martin Luther King led the boycott and became the spokesman of nonviolent resistance to racial segregation. In November 1956 the Supreme Court declared segregation on buses unconstitutional. The success encouraged sit-ins, freedom rides and the March on Washington in 1963, which led to the civil rights and voting rights acts of 1964 and 1965.

title: Launch of Sputnik 1
summary: The Soviet Union sends the first artificial satellite into space and triggers the Sputnik shock in the West.
text: On 4 October 1957 a Soviet rocket carried the 84-kilogram metal sphere Sputnik into orbit around the earth; radio amateurs all over the world could pick up its beeping. For the United States this was a shock, because the same rocket could carry nuclear warheads across the ocean, and the Soviet Union appeared to be technically superior. In 1958 Washington founded the space agency NASA and invested massively in science and education. The race into space brought the first human being into space with Yuri Gagarin in 1961, the American Moon landing in 1969, and satellites for weather, television and navigation.

title: The Year of Africa
summary: In a single year 17 African colonies become independent states.
text: After Ghana under Kwame Nkrumah had gained independence in 1957 as the first colony south of the Sahara, France in 1960 released almost all of its African territories from Senegal to Madagascar into independence; Nigeria, Somalia and the Belgian Congo also became independent. The United Nations admitted 17 new members and adopted a declaration against colonialism. But the borders of the colonial era, weak institutions and the interference of the superpowers weighed on the young states: in the Congo a civil war broke out immediately, in the course of which the first prime minister Patrice Lumumba was murdered in 1961. The settler colonies in the south, such as Algeria, Angola and Rhodesia, still had to win their freedom in long wars.

title: Building of the Berlin Wall
summary: On 13 August 1961 the GDR seals off West Berlin and puts an end to the flight of its citizens to the West.
text: By 1961 almost three million people had left the GDR by way of open Berlin. With Moscow's consent, the SED leadership under Walter Ulbricht had streets torn up and barbed wire strung during the night of 13 August; a concrete wall with a death strip soon followed. Families were separated overnight, and at least 140 people died at the Berlin Wall. It became the symbol of the Cold War and of the division of Europe.

title: Cuban Missile Crisis
summary: Soviet missiles in Cuba bring the world to the brink of nuclear war for thirteen days.
text: In October 1962 American reconnaissance aircraft discovered launch pads for Soviet medium-range missiles in Cuba. President Kennedy imposed a naval blockade and demanded their withdrawal. After days of tension Khrushchev gave in; in return the United States pledged not to attack Cuba and secretly withdrew missiles from Turkey. The crisis led to the establishment of the hotline between Washington and Moscow and, in 1963, to the first agreement on nuclear testing.

title: Vietnam War
summary: The United States intervenes in Vietnam with hundreds of thousands of soldiers and suffers its first defeat in a war.
text: After the victory of the Viet Minh over France in 1954, Vietnam was divided into a communist North under Ho Chi Minh and a South supported by the West. In order to halt the advance of communism in Southeast Asia, the United States sent ground troops from March 1965 onward and bombed the North; at the peak more than 500,000 American soldiers were in the country. Despite superior technology they were unable to defeat the Viet Cong guerrillas, and the television images of napalm and destroyed villages provoked protests worldwide. In 1973 the United States withdrew, and in 1975 the North took Saigon and united the country. Around 58,000 Americans and several million Vietnamese lost their lives.

title: Cultural Revolution in China
summary: Mao Zedong mobilizes the young against the party, intellectuals and traditions; terror and chaos grip the country.
text: In order to regain the power he had lost after the failed Great Leap Forward, Mao called on young people in 1966 to fight against bourgeois ideas and alleged traitors within the party. Millions of Red Guards waved the Little Red Book, publicly humiliated teachers, officials and artists, destroyed temples and books and deported the educated to the countryside for re-education; Deng Xiaoping too was stripped of power, and head of state Liu Shaoqi died in custody. Schools and universities remained closed for years, and the economy collapsed. Only Mao's death and the arrest of the Gang of Four in 1976 brought an end to the decade, which by some estimates cost more than a million lives. In 1981 the party declared it a catastrophe, but forbade any open examination of it.

title: Prague Spring and the Year of Protest 1968
summary: Warsaw Pact troops stifle the attempt at reform in Czechoslovakia, while in the West students rebel.
text: Under its new party leader Alexander Dubček, Czechoslovakia attempted from January 1968 to create a socialism with a human face: censorship was lifted, travel permitted and economic reforms begun. During the night of 21 August around half a million soldiers of the Soviet Union and its allies marched in; the population offered nonviolent resistance, but the reforms were reversed, and the Brezhnev Doctrine declared such intervention to be the rule. In the same year students protested in Paris, Berlin, Berkeley and Mexico City against the Vietnam War, authoritarian structures and the silence of their parents' generation. 1968 became the symbol of a generation of new departures that changed society, universities and political culture.

title: Moon Landing
summary: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin become the first people to set foot on the Moon.
text: After the Soviet Union had led the race into space with Sputnik in 1957 and Yuri Gagarin in 1961, Kennedy promised to put a human being on the Moon before the end of the decade. On 20 July 1969 the lunar module of Apollo 11 landed; around 600 million people watched live as Armstrong stepped onto the Moon. Five further landings followed up to 1972. The program brought advances in computer technology, materials and communications.

title: Oil Crisis
summary: The Arab oil states cut production; prices quadruple, and the economic miracle comes to an end.
text: During the Yom Kippur War in October 1973 the Arab OPEC states used oil as a political weapon against the supporters of Israel. In Western Europe and the United States there were fuel shortages, car-free Sundays and speed limits; inflation and unemployment rose. The crisis brought the postwar boom to an end and put energy saving, nuclear power and renewable energies on the political agenda.

title: Iranian Revolution
summary: The overthrow of the Shah turns Iran into an Islamic republic under Ayatollah Khomeini.
text: In 1978 millions of Iranians took to the streets against the dictatorship, the westernization and the social inequality under Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi; clergy, students, merchants and the left united in protest. In January 1979 the Shah left the country, in February the cleric Ruhollah Khomeini returned from exile and had an Islamic republic proclaimed by referendum, in which the word of the supreme religious leader stands above all laws. The occupation of the American embassy in Tehran, with 444 days of hostage-taking, destroyed relations with the United States, and the Iraqi attack in 1980 led to an eight-year war. The revolution gave political Islam a boost worldwide and triggered the second oil crisis.

title: Chernobyl Nuclear Disaster
summary: The explosion of a Soviet nuclear reactor contaminates large parts of Europe with radiation and shakes confidence in nuclear power.
text: During a botched test on 26 April 1986, reactor block 4 of the Chernobyl nuclear power plant in Ukraine exploded; burning graphite hurled radioactive material kilometers into the air. The Soviet leadership kept silent for days, and only measurements in Sweden forced it to disclose what had happened; the town of Pripyat and a zone of 30 kilometers were evacuated, and hundreds of thousands of clean-up workers were exposed to high levels of radiation. The radioactive cloud came down over Belarus, Scandinavia and Central Europe, where playgrounds were closed off and vegetables destroyed. The disaster reinforced Gorbachev's policy of openness, strengthened the anti-nuclear movement and led several countries to phase out nuclear energy.

title: Fall of the Berlin Wall
summary: On 9 November 1989 the GDR opens the border; the peaceful revolution puts an end to the division of Germany.
text: Mass flight by way of Hungary and the Monday demonstrations in Leipzig put the SED leadership under pressure in the autumn of 1989. When politburo member Günter Schabowski announced new travel regulations on the evening of 9 November, tens of thousands streamed to the border crossings, and the border guards raised the barriers. The communist regimes also fell in Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia and Romania. On 3 October 1990 the GDR acceded to the Federal Republic.

title: Dissolution of the Soviet Union
summary: The Soviet Union breaks apart into fifteen independent states; the Cold War is over.
text: Gorbachev's reforms had created freedoms but had not solved the economic crisis; the Baltic republics and others demanded independence. In August 1991 a coup by communist hardliners failed against the resistance gathered around Boris Yeltsin. On 8 December Russia, Ukraine and Belarus declared the union dissolved, and on 25 December Gorbachev resigned. Russia took over the legacy of the Soviet Union, including its nuclear weapons and its seat on the Security Council.

title: The World Wide Web Goes Public
summary: Tim Berners-Lee puts the first website online at CERN and makes the internet usable for everyone.
text: Since the 1970s the internet had connected computers at universities and in the military, but it could be operated only by specialists. From 1989 onward the British physicist Tim Berners-Lee developed at the CERN research center near Geneva a system consisting of web addresses, the transfer protocol HTTP and the page language HTML, with which documents could be linked worldwide. In August 1991 he made the first website public, in 1993 CERN released the technology free of charge, and with the Mosaic browser its triumphal progress began. Within a few years search engines, online commerce and social networks came into being; today more than five billion people use the network, which has fundamentally changed the economy, politics and everyday life.

title: End of Apartheid and the Election of Mandela
summary: Nelson Mandela is elected president in South Africa's first free elections.
text: From 1948 onward South Africa's white minority had stripped the black majority of its rights and segregated it spatially through the system of apartheid. International sanctions, protests and the resistance of the ANC forced President de Klerk in 1990 to release Mandela and to repeal the racial laws. In April 1994 all South Africans were allowed to vote for the first time; the ANC won, and Mandela became president. A Truth and Reconciliation Commission examined the crimes of apartheid.

title: Genocide in Rwanda
summary: Within about 100 days Hutu militias murder some 800,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu while the world looks on.
text: The Belgian colonial power had divided the population of Rwanda into Hutu and Tutsi and favored the Tutsi minority; after independence in 1962 discrimination and violence changed direction. When President Habyarimana's aircraft was shot down on 6 April 1994, the army, militias and incited neighbors began a planned campaign of murder, spurred on by radio stations that described the Tutsi as cockroaches. By July around 800,000 people had been killed with machetes and rifles, many of them in churches and schools to which they had fled. The United Nations even withdrew its blue helmets. Only the advance of the Tutsi rebels under Paul Kagame brought the killing to an end. An international tribunal later convicted those responsible, and the failure of the world community still shapes the debate about the responsibility to protect.

title: Attacks of 11 September
summary: Islamist terrorists fly hijacked aircraft into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon.
text: On 11 September 2001 nineteen attackers from the terrorist network al-Qaeda hijacked four passenger aircraft. Two brought down the Twin Towers in New York, one struck the Pentagon, and the fourth crashed in Pennsylvania after the passengers resisted. Almost 3,000 people died. The United States declared the war on terror, overthrew the Taliban regime in Afghanistan and invaded Iraq in 2003. Security checks and surveillance changed life all over the world.

title: Introduction of Euro Cash
summary: In twelve EU states euro coins and notes replace the national currencies.
text: The euro had been introduced as book money in 1999; on 1 January 2002 it came into circulation as cash and replaced the deutschmark, the franc, the lira and other currencies. Around 300 million people received a common currency that made trade and travel in Europe easier. The euro crisis from 2010 onward revealed the weaknesses of a currency without a common fiscal policy. Today more than 20 states use the euro.

title: Global Financial Crisis
summary: The collapse of the bank Lehman Brothers triggers the most severe economic crisis since 1929.
text: American banks had bundled risky mortgage loans into securities and sold them around the world. When property prices fell, the financial system began to totter; on 15 September 2008 Lehman Brothers went bankrupt. Governments rescued banks with hundreds of billions, the world economy contracted, and millions lost their jobs and their homes. The crisis led to stricter banking rules and fed mistrust of elites and of globalization.

title: Arab Spring
summary: Mass protests topple dictators in Tunisia, Egypt and Libya, but in many places lead to war and new repression.
text: The self-immolation of a vegetable seller in Tunisia in December 2010 set off protests against poverty, corruption and oppression that spread through social media across the entire Arab world. In Tunisia and Egypt the presidents resigned, and in Libya Gaddafi was overthrown. In Syria the uprising developed into a civil war with hundreds of thousands dead and millions of refugees. Only Tunisia remained on a democratic path for longer.

title: COVID-19 Pandemic
summary: A novel coronavirus spreads across the world; lockdowns and vaccination campaigns shape two years.
text: At the end of 2019 the virus SARS-CoV-2 appeared in the Chinese city of Wuhan; in March 2020 the World Health Organization declared a pandemic. Governments closed schools, shops and borders, public life came to a temporary standstill, and working from home and video conferences became part of everyday life. Within a year vaccines were developed and billions of doses were administered worldwide. According to WHO estimates, around 20 million people died of or with COVID-19 by 2023.

title: Russian Attack on Ukraine
summary: On 24 February 2022 Russia invades Ukraine and begins the largest war in Europe since 1945.
text: After the annexation of Crimea in 2014 and the war in the Donbas, President Vladimir Putin ordered the attack on the whole of the neighboring country on 24 February 2022, a country he regards as part of Russia and wanted to remove from the sphere of influence of the West. The swift victory he expected did not come about: the Ukrainian army and population defended Kyiv, and when the Russians withdrew, massacres of civilians were discovered in Bucha and other places. The Western states imposed unprecedented sanctions and supplied weapons, Finland and Sweden joined NATO, and millions of Ukrainians fled to Europe. With hundreds of thousands killed and wounded, cities destroyed and energy and food prices rising worldwide, the war put an end to hopes of a lasting peaceful order in Europe.
